What follows is a longer picture that includes the same men in a storm, and the picture gives them movement even while their eyes remain closed.

**SEALED SENSES LEAVE NO ROAD HOME**

Think of a man who nails his windows shut against a noise he dislikes and then complains that the house has no air. The verse describes the same arrangement in the matter of hearing, and it treats the closed windows as his own work. These days the instruments are fed or starved by what a person chooses to read, watch and repeat, and the passage tells him what happens to equipment that is never used for the purpose it was given. Nobody is asked to despise the men in the picture, and the reader is asked instead to notice that their road began with small refusals which each looked reasonable at the time. A person who can trace the first of those refusals in his own record is in a better position than one who only recognises it in a stranger. The sūrah turns next to the second picture, which shows the same people caught in weather they cannot manage, and the change in the image is a change in the kind of danger that surrounds them.

---

## Verse 2:19

> Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺

**STORM FROM ABOVE AND FEAR WITHIN**

The sūrah gives a second picture for the same people, and this one puts them in the middle of a night storm: ***“Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder”***, ***“and lightning”***. The early teachers read the storm as the revelation itself, since the rain that gives life is a fitting image for the Book that came down, and they read the darkness, the thunder and the flash as the doubts, the warnings and the moments of clarity that accompany it. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah are credited with readings of this kind, in which the rain is the Qur'an, the darkness is their confusion, and the thunderclaps are the commands and prohibitions that strike the ear. The picture is placed after the first one for a reason, since the man with the borrowed lantern has lost his light, while the people of this picture are still travelling through a storm that gives them light in flashes. Both are descriptions of the same disease at different stages, and the sūrah wants the reader to hold both.

**THE GESTURE OF THE FRIGHTENED TRAVELLERS**

The middle of the verse describes what the people in the storm do: ***“They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap”***, ***“for fear of death.”***. The gesture is exact and it is not mocked anywhere in the sentence, which is worth noticing in a passage about pretenders. Ibn ʿAbbās described the men as stopping their ears against the sound that frightened them, and the Book records the same reaction elsewhere in the language of the people who refused what they heard. The reason the picture works is that it shows belief and fear existing together in the same person, which is the condition of the pretender exactly: he is close enough to the message to be shaken by it and far enough from it to hope it passes. The Book describes the thunder itself as a creature that praises its Lord, which means the storm that frightens them is doing the work of its Maker while they crouch in it: (13:13 — **“The thunder glorifies His praises, as do the angels in awe of Him”**).

**DIVINE POWER SURROUNDS THE REFUSERS**

The verse ends with a statement that stops the reader from thinking the men are out of reach: ***“And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺”***. The wording describes a power that surrounds the people it deals with, and the sentence is placed after the account of their running and hiding. The Book describes the same surrounding elsewhere when it speaks about the flash of the cloud and the power behind it: (24:43 — **“The flash of the clouds' lightning nearly takes away eyesight”**). The early teachers read the closing as a warning to the men themselves rather than as a comfort to the community, since the hiding in the verse is useless against the One who sent the storm. What turns on the sentence is that fear is not the same as faith, and a person can be frightened by the truth for years without ever submitting to it. The next verse stays with the same travellers and shows what they do when the light appears, which is the most honest part of the whole description.

**A FIELD WITH A LAMP THAT FLASHES**

Think of a group crossing a field at night while a storm throws a flash of light every few minutes. Each flash shows the path ahead, and each one reveals how far off the track they had drifted when it was dark. The people of this picture walk in the flashes and stand still in the intervals, which is a portrait of a person who acts on the truth when it moves him and stops when the feeling passes. These days a reader may find the same pattern in his own week, since a reminder can produce a burst of effort and the following silence can produce nothing at all. The verse does not remove the storm and it does not promise that the storm will end soon; it shows the men in it, and the reader who recognises the description has been told where he is standing.

---

## Verse 2:20

> It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE LIGHT THAT COMES AND GOES**

The verse continues the storm and turns to what the lightning does to the people caught in it: ***“It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight”***. The wording describes a flash so strong that the men expect to lose their eyes with it, and the earliest authorities kept the comparison for the terror the revelation produced in the hearts of people who had set themselves against it. The flash, in a reading carried from Ibn ʿAbbās, stands for the moments when truth is shown plainly to the pretenders, while the thunder stands for the warnings that follow, and the description of the eye as the thing nearly taken away belongs to the same picture. The Book uses the same image for the lightning in another sūrah where its effect is described in a single phrase: (24:43 — **“The flash of the clouds' lightning nearly takes away eyesight”**). The picture therefore joins the storm of the previous verse and carries it further, since the danger has moved from the ears to the eyes.

**MOVEMENT ONLY WHILE THE FLASH LASTS**

The verse then records the two things the men do: ***“Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still”***. The sentence states the rhythm of a person who moves only when he is carried by an emotion and stops the moment it has gone, and the transmitted reading takes the walking as the small amount of good such people do while the flash lasts. The Book draws the line between the people who walk in steady light and those who move in fits in another sūrah where the two groups are shown at the end of the road: (57:12 — **“with their light shining ahead of them and on their right”**). The contrast is exact, because the light of the believers is described as their own for the journey and shining before them, while the light of this passage comes in flashes that reveal and then vanish. What turns on the difference is the state of the lamp inside the man rather than the brightness of the weather around him.

**POWER OVER EVERY FACULTY**

The verse closes with a statement about power that is aimed at the men in the picture: ***“Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight”***. The sentence names the two instruments and connects them to the same will that was behind the loss of the light, and it states the matter as a possibility that was not carried out. The Book uses the closing formula of the verse in another place where a great matter is described, and the wording there is worth placing beside it: (16:77 — **“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”**). The earliest teachers explained the verse as a reminder that the respite is itself a mercy, since the men had deserved the loss of the instruments in this life and were given time instead. That is the reason the sentence follows the account of their hiding, because the Book is telling them that the storm they are dodging could have finished the matter long before. The words that end it, ***“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***, are the same words the Book uses when it describes the Hour arriving in the blink of an eye.

**A SAILOR WHO SAILS BY THE FLASHES**

Think of a sailor who steers only when a flash of lightning shows him the rocks, and who drops his hands from the wheel the moment the sky goes dark. He will hit the rocks in one of the intervals, and the reason is not the dark or the flash but his own refusal to hold a course. The verse describes this kind of sailor with the respect that comes from truthfulness, since it does not pretend that the flashes were useless: the men did walk, and the walking is recorded. These days a reader can find the same pattern in a life built around the high moments of a season and the flat weeks between them, and the sūrah offers no remedy here beyond the portrait itself. The long account of the pretenders ends with this verse, and the sūrah then turns to address the readers as a community of worshippers, which is the subject of the verses that follow.

---

## Verse 2:21

> O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺

**AN ADDRESS TO EVERY HUMAN BEING**

After the long account of the pretenders, the address widens to the whole of humanity: ***“O humanity! Worship your Lord”***. The address is wider than the two groups described before it, and it reaches the readers of the Book in every generation along with the community that first heard it. ʿAlqamah and Mujāhid are credited with the observation that every address in the Book beginning with this phrase was revealed in Mecca, while the direct address to believers belongs to Madinah, which places this command among the earliest of the sūrah's sentences in order of revelation. Ibn ʿAbbās read the call as directed at the people of Mecca and also, in another report, at the people of the Scripture, and the two readings show how wide the door is meant to stand. The command is not addressed to a rank of scholars or to a nation with a claim on God; it is addressed to the species.

**WORSHIP GATHERS EVERY ACT OF SERVICE**

The command is followed by the word for worship, and Ibn ʿAbbās gave the reading that in the Book the word carries the sense of declaring God one and alone. That reading keeps the sentence from shrinking into ritual, since the first thing worship asks of a person is that he settle who God is. The Book states the purpose of the whole creation in the same terms in another sūrah, and the sentence there would fit here without a change: (51:56 — **“I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me”**). The reasoning that joins the two verses is the difference between a servant who performs a duty and a creature who exists for a purpose, and the verse in this sūrah is asking for the second understanding. That is why the command is placed before the account of the gifts that follows, because the gifts are the evidence and the worship is the answer.

**THE ARGUMENT FROM THE GENERATIONS BEHIND HIM**

The verse attaches the command to the act that made the commanded possible: ***“Who created you and those before you”***. The argument moves from the person in front of the sentence to the generations who stood in the same place and passed away, and it leaves the hearer with a lineage of creatures who were all brought into being by the same hand. The Book puts the same argument in the form of a question in another sūrah: (52:35 — **“Or were they created by nothing, or are they ˹their own˺ creators”**). The reason the second half of the phrase matters is that a person can allow a claim for his own existence and no further, and the verse widens the claim to everything that came before him. The reader is shown a chain whose beginning he cannot see, and he is told that the One who made the chain is the One he is being called to serve.

**THE PURPOSE NAMED IN THE LAST WORDS**

The verse closes with the object of the command, and the wording is one of purpose: ***“so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺”***. The devout scholars noticed the shape of the expression, since hope is not a quality that belongs to God in the way it belongs to a creature, and they explained it as a promise in the form of an aim, so that the servant knows what the command is intended to produce in him. The Book names the same quality as the fruit of worship in a hundred places, and the sūrah itself opened by naming the mindful as the people who would be guided. The point is that the command is not aimed at producing a performance but at forming a person, which is a difference worth keeping. The Book names the same quality as the mark of the people it addresses when it speaks to the believers in another sūrah: (3:102 — **“Be mindful of Allah in the way He deserves”**). Think of a teacher who sets an exercise not to fill an hour but to leave the student with a habit of mind; the command here works in the same way, and it can be repeated today for the same result in anyone who answers it.

---

## Verse 2:22

> ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺

**THE GIFTS THAT ANSWER THE COMMAND OF THE VERSE BEFORE**

The command to worship is followed by a list of what the Lord has already done, and the list opens with the One being named: ***“˹He is the One˺”***, ***“Who has made the earth a place”***, ***“of settlement”***, ***“for you and the sky a canopy”***. The first gift is a ground that carries the weight of a life, and the phrase describes a floor that was made fit for dwelling rather than left as a hazard. Ibn ʿAbbās and others explained the canopy as a roof over the earth, raised without pillars and guarded from falling, and the picture is one of a house rather than of a wilderness. The Book states the same pair of gifts in another sūrah with almost the same words, and its repetition marks a settled description of God's dealing with the human being: (40:64 — **“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy”**).

**THE PROVISION THAT COMES DOWN AND COMES OUT**

The list widens to the rain and to what it produces: ***“and sends down rain from the sky,”***, ***“causing fruits to grow”***, ***“as a provision for you.”***. The order of the sentence is the order of a person's dependence, since the water arrives before the fruit and the fruit arrives before the eater knows he will need it. The Book repeats the same chain elsewhere as a reminder of where the arrangement comes from: (14:32 — **“causing fruits to grow as a provision for you”**). The phrase about provision covers everything a person lives on, whether he earned it by work or received it without work, and the wording leaves the credit with the sender of the rain. That is why the sentence does not mention farmers or markets, because the arrangement is older than either of them and larger than both. What turns on the sentence for the reader is that a man may spend his life producing food and never once look past the market to the chain that brought it, and the verse makes the chain visible in a single line.

**EQUALS FORBIDDEN AFTER THE GIFTS**

The verse closes with a prohibition attached to all that came before it: ***“So do not knowingly set up equals”***, ***“to Allah ˹in worship˺”***. The word for knowledge in the middle of the sentence is doing real work, since it removes ignorance as an excuse and leaves the hearer with what he already knows. The Book uses the same charge in a question that puts the whole matter in one line: (41:9 — **“And how can you set up equals with Him?”**). The reason the prohibition is placed after the gifts rather than before them is that the gifts are the proof, and a person who has received a house, a roof and food from one hand cannot plead that he did not know whose the hand was. Ibn ʿAbbās read the closing as a warning to those who knew the truth about God's oneness and still gave a share of their worship to something else, and the sūrah keeps that reading in view in the verses that follow. What turns on the word for knowledge is that the excuse of a person who never heard does not survive it, since the reader of this verse has heard the argument and can no longer claim the benefit of the doubt.

**A CHILD WHO THANKS THE WELL FOR THE WATER**

Think of a child who is brought water from the well by his father and thanks the well for it. The gratitude is real and the direction is wrong, and the mistake costs nothing until the day someone asks the child who built the well. The verse makes the same correction with the whole of a human life, and it does it by naming the gifts before it names the error, which is the way a good teacher corrects a student. These days a person can live inside a system of provision so efficient that the sender disappears behind the machinery, and the passage asks him to look up from the machinery once. Nobody is asked to despise the means; the child is asked to know whose hands carried the water, and the knowledge is what the next verse puts to the test with a challenge that no rival of God has ever answered.

---

## Verse 2:23

> And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true

**DOUBT INVITED TO PRODUCE ITS PROOF**

After naming the gifts, the sūrah turns to the message itself and answers a doubt with an invitation to test it: ***“And if you are in doubt about”***, ***“what We have revealed to Our servant,”***. The servant named here is the Prophet, and the title is worth noticing, because the Book calls him a servant at the moment it stakes everything on the revelation he carries. Ibn ʿAbbās and the earliest teachers read the doubt as belonging to the pretenders and to those who had heard the message and hesitated, and the verse does not treat the doubt as a crime in itself. The Book states the same invitation in two other sūrahs with the number of sūrahs they were asked to produce named in each, which shows that the challenge was repeated as the message was repeated. What turns on the wording is that the reader is not asked to swallow the claim; he is told to test it with the tools he already has.

**WHAT THEY WERE TOLD TO BRING**

The invitation is specific: ***“then produce a sûrah like it”***. The demand is not for a book or for a poem but for something of the same kind as the shortest unit of what had been revealed, which means the challenge stands within the reach of anyone with a language and a claim. The Book repeats the same demand in two places with the helpers and the honesty clause attached, and one of them shows exactly how much help the challengers were permitted to gather: (10:38 — **“Produce one sûrah like it then, and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!”**). A later sūrah widens the field to include every human being and every jinn, which removes the excuse of a small tribe in a small country: (17:88 — **“they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported each other”**). The reason the challenge is confined to a single unit is that the claim being tested is specific, and the test is meant to be answerable rather than impossible.

**THE HELPERS THEY WERE TOLD TO CALL**

The verse allows the doubters to bring support: ***“and call your helpers other than Allah”***, ***“if what you say is true”***. The last clause places the whole matter under the truthfulness of the people making the claim, and the Book uses the same clause at the end of the other two versions of the challenge. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the helpers as the deities the doubters called on for support, and others took them as the witnesses and the men of eloquence whose testimony they were relying on. The reason the verse does not forbid them to consult anyone outside God is that the point is already decided by the invitation, since no ally of theirs can supply what the challenge requires. A reader who has ever been challenged to match a piece of work knows the difference between an open test and a closed one, and this one is left open on purpose so that the failure cannot be blamed on the rules. The people who took up the challenge left no sūrah behind, and the silence has held for fourteen centuries, which is the answer the verse was waiting for when it named the clause.

**A CRAFTSMAN WHO DARES THE TOWN TO COPY HIS WORK**

Think of a potter who sets a bowl in the market and tells every potter in the town to make its match, offering to pay for the clay and to allow any tool they like. The offer would be pointless in a market where a hundred men could do the work, and it is decisive in one where none of them can. The verse makes the same offer with the message and with the whole of a community's talent, and the offer has been open ever since. These days the text is available to more readers and in more languages than at any point in its history, and the invitation stands where it stood, which is why the doubt of a modern reader is met with the same test as the doubt of the first hearer. A person who takes the challenge seriously will read the Book with the question in his hands rather than with a verdict already written, and the sūrah leaves him free to do exactly that.

---

## Verse 2:24

> But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers

**A VERDICT PRONOUNCED BEFORE THE ATTEMPT**

The sūrah completes the test with a statement that turns it into a verdict: ***“But if you are unable to do so”***, ***“and you will never be able to do so”***. The construction announces the outcome before the challengers have tried, and the scholars explain the shape of it in the same way they explained the earlier verse of purpose: a condition spoken by God is not an expression of uncertainty but a statement of what will happen. The challenge was put to the pagans, the Jews and the Christians together, which means the test was offered to every community in the region that had a claim to a revelation and a reason to doubt this one. The wording is a prophecy before it is anything else, and the history of the text since that day has kept it standing. That is why the sūrah moves straight from the test to the consequence, because a challenge that cannot be met has finished its work. A doubter may still hold his doubt, and the sentence has told him in advance that the doubt is not something the text will lose sleep over.

**THE FIRE THAT WAS MADE READY**

The consequence is named without decoration: ***“then fear the Fire fuelled with people”***, ***“and stones, which is prepared”***, ***“for the disbelievers”***. The verse describes the punishment as something standing ready rather than as something to be arranged later, and the wording about its fuel is exact. The early teachers read the people as the disbelievers themselves, and the stones either as the idols that were worshipped or as a material that burns far hotter than wood, which is how they explained the intensity of the fire. The reading from Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the stones as the idols themselves, and the Book makes that reading explicit in another sūrah where the objects of worship are named as fuel beside the people who served them: (21:98 — **“you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell”**). The Book repeats the same phrase in a command to the believers a few sūrahs later, where they are told to shield their families from it: (66:6 — **“a Fire whose fuel is people and stones”**).

**CERTAINTY AFTER THE FAILED CHALLENGE**

The order of the two verses is part of the argument, and the reason is worth stating plainly. The sūrah first offers the doubters a way of testing the message with their own abilities, then tells them that the test will not be passed, and then sends them to the consequence with their eyes open. A person who has been shown that the text is beyond him has no ground left for treating the matter as an opinion he may sample at leisure, because the claim he is dismissing has proved itself in the only arena he asked for. The Book uses the same sequence elsewhere when it challenges the doubters to bring ten sūrahs and then states the failure they will meet: (11:13 — **“Produce ten fabricated sûrahs like it and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!”**). What turns on the sequence is that the warning is aimed at a person who has already been given his chance rather than at a stranger who never heard.

**WRITTEN NOTICE BEFORE THE BLAZE**

Think of a traveller who reaches a bridge with a warning board signed by the engineer who built it, and who decides that the board is the opinion of an interested party. The bridge does not fail because he doubted it, and it does not wait for his book of reasons either. The verse treats the message in the same way, and it gives the reader the test first and the consequence afterwards, which is the fairest order the matter can have. These days a person may live inside a culture where every claim is treated as one option among many, and this verse asks him to notice that some claims have been tested in the way he would have chosen to test them. The next verse turns from the warning to the good news, and the sūrah shows that the same Book that leaves the doubter without an excuse gives the believer more than he asked for.

---

## Verse 2:25

> Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,” for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺. They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever

**THE GOOD NEWS THAT ANSWERS THE WARNING**

Good news stands directly across from the warning about the Fire: ***“Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good”***. The two marks are named together, faith and the work that follows it, which is the same pairing the sūrah used at its head. Ibn ʿAbbās read the believing as faith in the messenger and the Book, and the good work as the obedience that binds a person to his Lord, while others read the second phrase as covering every righteous act a person performs. The Book places the promise here immediately after the threat of the fire, so the two ends can be weighed as the two prices of the same choice. The news is commanded before it is described, which means the messenger is told to carry it to the people who earned it, and the sūrah treats the announcement itself as part of the mercy.

**THE GARDENS AND THE RIVERS BENEATH THEM**

The promise is then given its shape: ***“that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow.”***. The image is a garden with water running beneath the trees, and the early teachers named the rivers as water, milk, honey and wine, which the Book lists in a later sūrah where the whole garden is described: (47:15 — **“in it are rivers of fresh water, rivers of milk that never changes in taste”**). The reason the promise is given in the language of a garden is that the first hearers lived in a country where water made the difference between life and death, and the Book speaks to them in the terms of the thing they most desired. The wording about the rivers describes them as flowing rather than as standing, which means the garden is not a single gift received once but a provision that keeps arriving. A reader who has seen a stream run through a dry valley knows why the picture was chosen for the reward.

**THE FRUIT THAT LOOKS FAMILIAR AND TASTES NEW**

The verse then describes a conversation inside the garden: ***“Whenever provided with fruit, they will say,”***, ***“This is what we were given before,”***. The sentence records the surprise of people who recognise the shape of what they are handed and find the taste beyond anything they knew. The verse explains the recognition in the words that follow: ***“for they will be served fruit”***, ***“that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās explained the resemblance as a likeness in appearance and colour and not in taste, and another reading applies it to the fruits of this world which the people of the garden remember as similar in form while the new ones exceed them. The Book states the same abundance in a description that closes the picture with a promise that nothing there runs out: (13:35 — **“eternal is its fruit as well as its shade”**). The reason the sentence is placed here is that a reward a person cannot imagine is a reward he cannot want, so the Book grants the familiar form and keeps the newness in the taste. A reader who has tasted two kinds of the same fruit will understand the arrangement, since the eye is satisfied by the look and the tongue is left with the surprise.

**THE SPOUSES AND THE FOREVER**

The verse finishes with two more gifts: ***“They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever”***. The purity is explained by the early teachers as a freedom from everything that spoils company in this life, and the permanence is stated as plainly as the rest of the promise. The Book uses the same word for the lasting stay in several places, and the sūrah makes it the last note of the good news so that the reader ends the sentence with the thought that nothing he receives there will be lost. Think of a guest who is told at the door that the meal is ready and that the room he is given is his for good; the second half of that sentence is what makes the first half safe to enjoy. These days a person holds every good thing in his life with the knowledge that it will end, which is the reason the promise ends on the word forever, and the reader is invited to want a gift that no loss can touch.

---

## Verse 2:26

> Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller. As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?” Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—

**THE OBJECTION TO THE PARABLES AND THE ANSWER TO IT**

The sūrah now answers a complaint that had been raised against its own method: ***“Surely Allah does not shy away from”***, ***“using the parable of a mosquito”***, ***“or what is even smaller.”***. The objection came from people who found the small creatures used in the Book's comparisons unworthy of a divine text, and the verse meets the objection by naming the smallest of them and then going below it. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās explains that God does not refrain from striking a comparison even with a gnat, and al-Suddī reported that the objection was raised when the parables about the pretenders in the earlier verses were recited. The early teachers also placed the objection in the mouths of the Jews who scoffed at the mention of a fly or a spider, and the Book answers all of them in one sentence. The reason the matter is worth a verse of its own is that the objection was not about a creature but about who decides what is fitting for revelation.

**WHAT A PARABLE IS FOR AND WHY SIZE IS IRRELEVANT**

The Book explains the purpose of its comparisons in a verse that makes the answer plain: (29:43 — **“These are the parables We set forth for humanity, but none will understand them except the people of knowledge”**). A parable is a tool for carrying a meaning into a mind that would not hold it in its abstract form, and the tool is chosen for the work rather than for its dignity. The Book uses the lowliest things in creation when they carry the point best, and it uses the loftiest, such as the light of the heavens, when the subject calls for that. The reasoning behind the answer is that the objection confused the size of the example with the weight of the meaning, which is like refusing a key because it is smaller than the door. What turns on the sentence for the reader is that he should meet a comparison in the Book by asking what it teaches rather than by asking whether the subject of it was respectable.

**HOW THE SAME WORDS ARE RECEIVED**

The verse then divides its hearers by what they do with the same words: ***“As for the believers, they know”***, ***“that it is the truth from their”***, ***“Lord.”***, ***“And as for the disbelievers, they argue”***, ***“What does Allah mean by such a”***, ***“parable?”***. The believers are described as knowing, and the disbelievers as arguing, and the two reactions come from the same sentence read by two different hearts. The Book describes the same split in another place where the comparisons are said to be set out for people who may reflect on them: (14:25 — **“This is how Allah sets forth parables for the people, so perhaps they will be mindful”**). The reason a parable can guide one person and unsettle another is that it is a test of what a person wants from the text, and the verse says as much in its next words. The reader who finds himself annoyed by a comparison has been given a small window into his own state, and the sūrah treats that reaction as information rather than as an accident.

**THE STRAYING THAT IS MENTIONED HERE**

The verse closes with a statement that has disturbed some readers: ***“Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many”***, ***“to stray”***, ***“and guides many. And He leaves none”***, ***“to stray except the rebellious”***. The sentence ties the leaving to the test and the rebellion to the people who take the road, and the last words name the character of the people being described. The Book explains the same leaving in another sūrah when it says that the comparison is understood by the people of knowledge and missed by the rest. The reason the verse can speak this way is that a person is not left without a route; he is left to the route he has chosen, and the words that follow in the next verse describe the men who break their covenants. The Book sets out the same test in another sūrah where the comparison is said to separate the people who reflect from the rest: (13:17 — **“This is how Allah sets forth parables”**). Both readings of the words agree on where the decision sits, since the text is the same for the two groups and the difference is in what each one brings to it. Think of a signpost that sends one traveller home and another into a ditch: the sign is the same and the difference is in the traveller, and the Book is content to let the reader decide which of the two he has been so far.  Today, a reader can still dismiss a small example while avoiding the large truth it exposes, because scale does not decide whether a comparison is sound.

---

## Verse 2:27

> those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land. It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers

**THE PARABLE IDENTIFIES ITS TRUE SUBJECTS**

The people exposed by the parable are now identified: ***“those who violate Allah's covenant after it”***, ***“has been affirmed”***. The word for violating carries the sense of breaking something that was sound, and the early teachers described the covenant as the binding agreement by which a person acknowledges his Lord. Ibn ʿAbbās read it as the covenant concerning the Prophet, taken from the communities through their books and their prophets, and another reading places it at the moment when every human being was asked to bear witness to his Lord. The Book states the same scene in a sūrah that records the answer of humanity at that moment, and the reader who keeps it in view understands why the verse treats the break as a violation rather than as a simple mistake. A person who has given his word has already been bound by it, and the sentence says so before it names any other offence. The point of naming the covenant first is that every other charge in the verse hangs on it, because the ties and the corruption are the visible form of the broken bond rather than separate crimes.

**BONDS THAT DIVINE COMMAND KEEPS INTACT**

The verse widens the charge to the relationships a person holds: ***“break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah”***, ***“has ordered to be maintained”***. The early teachers read the phrase as covering every bond the religion commands a person to keep, from the bond with God to the bond with parents, relatives and neighbours, and some of them noted that the word used here is about joining rather than about kindness, which makes the duty a matter of maintaining a connection. The Book names the same offence in another sūrah with a description of the offenders that follows it to its end: (13:25 — **“And those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained,”**). The reason the ties are named after the covenant is that a broken relationship with God shows itself first in the relationships a person can see, which is why the verse moves from the unseen bond to the visible ones in a single line. The order is the order of diagnosis, since a community cannot see what is in a man's heart and can see what he does to his neighbours.

**THE SPREADING OF CORRUPTION AND THE LOSS THAT FOLLOWS**

The charge closes with the same offence named earlier in the sūrah: ***“and spread corruption in the land. It”***, ***“is they”***, ***“who are the ˹true˺ losers”***. The sūrah has already described the pretenders as the corrupters of the community, and the verse here applies the description to the people who break their bonds, which shows that the two groups are the same in result if not in name. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the losing as the loss of this world and the next together, and the phrase carries the sense of a bargain in which a person's capital is gone. The Book states the same outcome for the men who traded their pledges for a small gain: (16:95 — **“And do not trade Allah's covenant for a fleeting gain”**). Here the loss is measured by what was given away and not by what was gained, since a man who sells a foundation for a handful of coins is poorer by the whole house. That is why the sentence ends with a verdict about the men rather than about the crime, because the Book is describing a condition that has already been reached.

**BROKEN BONDS BRING REAL LOSS**

Think of a man who takes the stones out of his own house's foundation to sell them, and who lives comfortably for a season on the price. The walls stand for a while because they were built well, and then the first storm shows what he did. The verse describes the same arrangement in the life of a person who breaks the bonds that hold his world together, and it calls the result a loss rather than a punishment in the first place. These days the ties in question are broken quietly, through absences, silences and paperwork, and the passage asks the reader to look at the foundation he is standing on. The next verses turn to the ground of the whole matter by asking the human being a question about his own beginning, and the question is one that nobody can answer except by admitting where he came from.

---

## Verse 2:28

> How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned

**LIFE ITSELF TESTIFIES AGAINST DENIAL**

A question addressed to the human being interrupts the description of the losers: ***“How can you deny Allah?”***. The question is not looking for information; it is pointing at a contradiction, and the contradiction is stated in the words that follow it. The early teachers read the sentence as addressed to everyone who hears it, and the sūrah has already spoken once to the whole of humanity in the same way, which means the question is meant for the reader and not only for the people of the first century. The Book asks a question of this kind in several places where a person's own existence is used as the proof against him, and the sūrah here does the same with the shortest possible account of a human life. A man who cannot explain how he came to be is in no position to explain away the One who brought him.

**THE LIFE THAT WAS GIVEN BEFORE IT WAS ASKED FOR**

The answer begins with the state the hearer was in: ***“You were lifeless and He gave you”***, ***“life”***. The wording puts the reader in the position of a thing that had no claim on existence and received it anyway. For Ibn ʿAbbās, the phrase described the human being before the breath was placed in him, and other early teachers took it as a description of the dust from which he was formed. The Book states the same act in another sūrah with the sentence that follows the gift to its next stage: (22:66 — **“And He is the One Who gave you life, then will cause you to die,”**). The reason the argument starts with the first gift rather than with the last is that the reader has already received the first one, and he is standing in the middle of an arrangement whose beginning he did not negotiate. What turns on the phrase is that gratitude for life itself is not a feeling the verse asks for; it is a fact the verse records.

**THE DEATH AND THE RETURN THAT HAVE NOT HAPPENED YET**

The verse continues through the two events that are still ahead of the reader: ***“then He will cause you to die”***, ***“and again bring you to life”***, ***“and then to Him you will ˹all˺”***, ***“be returned”***. The sentence names the whole course of a human being in one line, and it places the return to God at the end of it as the point where the account is settled. The Book repeats the same sequence in a passage that ends with a warning about ingratitude: (30:19 — **“And He gives life to the earth after its death. And so will you be brought forth ˹from the grave˺”**). It was noted among the earliest teachers that the dying and the raising are stated with the same certainty as the giving of life in the past, which means the future belongs to the same hand that has already acted. The reason the sentence reads as a list rather than as a threat is that every item in it has happened or will happen to the reader himself, and the list is simply his own life stated from the outside. A reader who has stood at the grave of someone he loved knows that the third event in this list is the one his whole life is arranged around, whether he admits it or not. The verse puts the return at the end of the sentence without a description of what waits there, because the fact of the return is enough to change how a person spends the interval.

**BORROWED LIFE POINTS BACK TO ITS GIVER**

Think of a passenger on a ship who is told that his passage was paid before he was born and that the same hand will settle the account at the end of the voyage. His only contribution is the way he spends the journey, and the question in the verse asks how such a man could deny the owner of the ship. These days a person can live with the sense that his existence is simply the ground under his feet, and the verse makes the ground itself an argument. The next verses continue the same account with the earth, the sky and the means of life, and they lead the reader to the place where the argument of the whole sūrah has been heading from its first page.

---

## Verse 2:29

> He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens. And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**THE EARTH THAT WAS FURNISHED BEFORE THE TENANT ARRIVED**

The argument of the previous verses continues with a statement about the world the reader lives in: ***“He is the One”***, ***“Who created everything in the earth”***, ***“for you.”***. The words put the whole of the ground under the reader's feet at his service, and its broad reach was understood to cover the animals, plants and materials on which human life depends. Ibn ʿAbbās described the sentence as a blessing stated in the form of a fact, and he read the creation of these things as an act of subservience granted before the tenant had done anything to deserve it. The Book names the same arrangement in a later passage where the gift is stated in the same form: (45:13 — **“He ˹also˺ subjected for you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth”**). That is why the verse is placed after the question about denying God, because a person who is surrounded by provision is being asked what he has done with it.

**HEAVEN ORDERED ABOVE A FURNISHED EARTH**

The verse moves from the ground to what stands above it: ***“Then He turned towards the”***, ***“heaven, forming it into seven heavens.”***. The early teachers discussed the turning with care, and the reading that carried the day among them is the one that gives the verb the sense of directing attention and purpose towards the heaven and shaping it as a builder shapes a roof. Ibn ʿAbbās read the forming as the arranging of the heavens in their layers, one above another, which is how the Book describes them in a sūrah where they are named as a structure with no fault in it: (67:3 — **“˹He is the One˺ Who created seven heavens, one above the other”**). The reason the number is stated rather than left to the imagination is that the reader is being told that the sky is not a void but an order, and an order is evidence of the One who arranged it. The verse does not describe what lies inside those heavens, since its business here is the fact of the making rather than the furniture of the made.

**THE KNOWLEDGE THAT CLOSES THE SENTENCE**

The verse ends with a statement that covers everything the reader has just been told: ***“And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge”***, ***“of all things”***. The early readers noticed that the sentence is placed after the account of the earth and the heavens rather than before it, and they explained the placing as a way of joining the two facts: the One who made all of it is the One who knows all of it. The Book states the same pair in a passage about the making of the heavens, where the shaping and the knowledge are named in a single verse: (41:12 — **“So He formed the heaven into seven heavens in two Days”**). The reason the sentence matters for the reader is that a maker who does not know his work is a maker who has lost interest in it, and the verse denies the reader that unhappy picture before he can form it. What turns on the words is the difference between a world that is running down without supervision and a world whose every part is held in the knowledge of its maker.

**A HOUSE PREPARED FOR A GUEST WHO HAS NOT KEPT IN TOUCH**

Think of a traveller who arrives at a house to find the table laid, the lamps lit and a bed made up in a room he has never seen, all arranged by a host he has not written to for years. The verse describes the reader as the guest in that house, and it puts the whole of the arrangement into one sentence. These days the same furnishings are hidden behind the labels of science and industry, which describe how the table was laid and rarely ask who laid it, and the passage asks the reader to notice the arrangement as a whole. The next verse goes further and shows a conversation about this very planet, which is where the sūrah begins the long account of the human being and what he was made for.

---

## Verse 2:30

> ˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.” They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?” Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.”

**THE ANNOUNCEMENT MADE TO THE ANGELS**

The sūrah now opens a scene from before the human being existed: ***“˹Remember˺ when your Lord said”***, ***“to the angels”***, ***“I am going to place a successive”***, ***“˹human˺ authority on earth.”***. The command to remember is addressed to the Prophet and, through him, to the reader, which means the scene is being shown for a purpose rather than told as a curiosity. The early teachers explained the word used for the appointment as a reference to one who acts on another's behalf, and they read the phrase about succession as covering generation after generation of human beings, each taking the place of the ones before. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others are credited with the reading that the appointment was a responsibility rather than a privilege, since a deputy answers to the one who sent him. The reason the scene is placed here, after the account of the earth being furnished for the human being, is that the furnishing and the appointment are two halves of one arrangement.

**ANGELIC CONCERN BEFORE THE APPOINTMENT**

The verse records the angels' question without any criticism of them: ***“They asked ˹Allah˺”***, ***“Will You place in it someone”***, ***“who will spread corruption there”***, ***“and shed blood”***. Their words show that they expected bloodshed from the creature being announced, and the early teachers explained their expectation in two ways, one taking it as knowledge given to them about what the human being would do and the other as a conclusion drawn from the record of an earlier creation that had done the same. A reading handed down from Ibn ʿAbbās treats the angels as seekers of information rather than objectors, and other teachers noted that their question came from care for the creation rather than from envy. The Book keeps their tone in the sentence that follows, which is the language of worship rather than of complaint, and the reader is left to weigh what that shows about how a question should be asked.

**THE WORSHIP THEY NAMED AS THEIR OWN**

The angelic question finishes with the statement that gives their words their weight: ***“while we glorify Your”***, ***“praises”***, ***“and proclaim Your holiness?”***. The two verbs describe continuous praise and the setting apart of God from every defect, and the angels offered both as their constant work. The Book records the same occupation in another sūrah where the angels are described in their ranks, and the sentence there shows what the reader should understand about their question. The reason the verse gives their worship in their own words is that it lets the reader see the two candidates for the earth side by side: a creature who would shed blood and a creature who never stops praising. What turns on the exchange is that the choice belonged to the One who made both, and the verse does not present the angels' argument as a mistake; it presents it as an argument that was answered from a knowledge they did not have.

**HIDDEN WISDOM BEHIND THE DECREE**

The verse ends with the answer of the Lord: ***“Allah responded”***, ***“I know what you do not know.”***. The sentence does not explain what the knowledge contains, and the sūrah leaves the reader to learn it from the rest of the account, which continues with the teaching of the names. The Book answers the same kind of question in another place where the wisdom behind the appointment is shown in the raising of a successor who repairs what others damaged: (6:165 — **“He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth”**). The reason the answer is given in this form is that a purpose can be known to its author and hidden from the instruments of the purpose, and the angels were instruments rather than partners. A reader who has ever been left without an explanation for a decision made above him has stood in the position of the angels here, and the verse does not treat that position as a fault. Think of a foreman who is told by the owner that a difficult workman is being hired, and who warns the owner about the mess the man will make; the owner's answer is that he knows more about the man than the foreman does, and the work goes ahead. The next verse shows the answer being filled in, and it begins with the names.  In a council today, limited knowledge can make a sound concern incomplete, which is why humility must remain after the concern has been voiced.

---

## Verse 2:31

> He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?”

**THE LESSON THAT SETTLED THE ARGUMENT**

The answer to the angels' question arrives in the form of a lesson: ***“He taught Adam the names”***, ***“of all things”***. The early teachers differed over what the names covered, and their readings are all worth knowing. Ibn ʿAbbās took them to be the names people use in ordinary speech, down to the pot and the plate, while Mujāhid read them as the names of everything that exists, and a third reading takes them as the names of the angels themselves. The difference between the readings does not touch the point of the verse, which is that knowledge was given to the human being that the angels did not have. The Book states the same gift of teaching in its earliest revelation, where the Lord is described as the one who taught by the pen: (96:4 — **“Who taught by the pen—”**). The gift recorded here is therefore not an episode in a single story but the pattern by which this creature was made to live, since he is the only one in the scene who is given a lesson. A reader who wonders what made this creature fit for the earth is given the answer in the first word of the sentence.

**THE PRESENTATION AND THE CHALLENGE THAT WENT WITH IT**

The verse then stages the test: ***“then He presented them to the angels”***, ***“and said”***, ***“Tell Me the names of these”***, ***“if what you say is true?”***. The last clause refers back to the claim the angels had made about their own worthiness, and the transmitted reading treats it as the reproach of a sincere claim made without the full picture. The Book continues the same scene in the verse that follows this one, where the command is given to Adam to inform the angels of the names: (2:33 — **“O Adam! Inform them of their names.”**). The reason the test is public rather than private is that the angels had spoken in public, and the honour of the human being had to be settled in the same assembly. What turns on the scene is that knowledge is the qualification for the appointment, and the verse lets the reader see how the qualification was granted rather than assuming it.

**THE VOICE THAT SPEAKS AGAIN IN THE NEXT VERSE**

The scene is left hanging at the end of this verse, since the angels have been asked for the names and the answer comes in the verse that follows. The pause is deliberate, and the reader who has followed the sūrah has already been told what the angels will say, because the sūrah recorded their earlier words about the worship of God. The Book uses the same technique of a suspended answer in the passage where the fire and its keepers are described, and the effect there is the same as here, which is to make the reader wait for a reply he cannot supply himself. The reason the question is left unanswered is that the angels' answer is worth hearing in full, since it becomes a model of how a creature should respond to a limit it cannot cross. The Book teaches by scenes like this one, and the reader who watches the angels handle a question they cannot answer is being taught something the command alone could not deliver. The reader who has his own limits in front of him is being shown the right posture before he is shown the correction.

**A STUDENT ASKED TO NAME THE TOOLS OF A TRADE**

Think of a workshop where the master asks his apprentices to name the tools on the bench, and where the newest boy is the only one who knows every one of them. The master does not shame the older apprentices; he shows them what the owner of the workshop had seen in the boy. The verse stages the same demonstration with the whole creation as the bench and the angels as the onlookers, and it does it to settle a question about worth. These days a person can measure himself by the noise of his claim and forget that the appointment in this world was given with a lesson attached, and the passage asks him what he has actually been taught in order to carry it. The sūrah goes on to record the answer of the angels, which is the answer a humble creature gives when the question is beyond him.

---

## Verse 2:32

> They replied, “Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

**CREATURELY KNOWLEDGE STOPS AT ITS BOUNDARY**

The angels reply with one of the shortest confessions in the Book: ***“They replied”***, ***“Glory be to You!”***. The word for glory declares God free of every defect, and the angels use it before they say anything about themselves, which means the correction they had received was accepted without argument. The early teachers pointed to this order as the model of how a creature should answer a charge: the majesty of God is acknowledged first, and the defence of the self comes afterwards and only as far as it is true. The Book records the same opening on the lips of other servants in other places, and the phrase is a standard by which a person's tone can be measured. The angels could have named their years of worship as a claim; instead they began by clearing their Lord of any injustice, and that difference deserves notice.

**CREATURELY LIMIT SPOKEN WITHOUT RESERVE**

The reply continues with a sentence that gives away the whole position: ***“We have no knowledge except what You”***, ***“have taught us.”***. The wording is absolute, and it was received as a confession that no creature owns knowledge as property; everything known is a loan that was granted. The angels, as Ibn ʿAbbās read their reply, admitted the boundary of their knowledge rather than making a plea, and the sūrah lets their words stand as an answer to the claim they had made about their own worthiness. The Book gives the same limit a voice in another sūrah, where the human being is told how much of the hidden he has been given: (17:85 — **“you ˹O humanity˺ have been given but little knowledge.”**). The angels' confession is the same admission made by a creature who has no interest in pretending to a rank he does not hold, and the sentence is short because a limit once admitted needs no decoration. What turns on the confession is that a creature's knowledge does not entitle him to rank; the One who gave it decides what it is for, which is the point the angels had missed when they weighed their worship against the coming creature.

**THE NAMES THAT CLOSE THE REPLY**

The Book uses the same absolution for a servant who cannot answer, since the admission of a limit is not a defeat in this register. The verse ends with the titles that explain why the answer is where it is: ***“You are truly the”***, ***“All-Knowing, All-Wise.”***. The first title covers the knowledge that the angels lacked and the second covers the arrangement they could not see, which means the reply has been answered by God's own description of Himself. The Book pairs knowledge and wisdom in several places where the arrangement of things is being explained, and the most famous of those places shows how far the knowledge reaches: (2:255 — **“no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺”**). The pairing is a summary of the whole scene, since the first name answers the question about what God knows and the second answers the question about what God is doing. The reason the angels call on wisdom as well as knowledge is that they had questioned not only what God knew but what He was doing, and the second name addresses the second half of their question. Think of a foreman who is told that the owner's decision was made with reasons he is not able to see, and who answers that the owner knows the site better than he does. The sentence is the same shape as the angels' reply, and it leaves the foreman with something to do rather than with a grievance to nurse. A person who works under an authority larger than his information has to decide whether he will serve with trust or with suspicion, and this verse shows a creature choosing trust after being corrected in public. These days a person can hold the same question about the way things are run, and the passage gives him the same answer plus the same lesson in how to pose it. Such restraint is knowledge in its proper form because it keeps a servant within the truth he has actually received.

---

## Verse 2:33

> Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.” Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”

**THE STUDENT IS ASKED, AND THE TEACHER SPEAKS AGAIN**

The examination ends, and the reader is shown the answer being given by the one who had been taught: ***“Allah said, “O Adam!”***, ***“Inform them of their names.””***, then ***“Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you”***, ***“that I know the secrets of the heavens”***, ***“and the earth, and I know what you reveal”***, ***“and what you conceal?””***. The command to Adam comes before the lesson is drawn, which is how the scene stays honest. The angels did not hear a claim about Adam's knowledge; they heard him name the things in front of them. Only after the demonstration does the Lord return to the exchange that opened the scene, and the question he asks is a reminder rather than a reproach. Qatādah carried this scene as a public display of what had been taught, which means Adam's answer served as evidence rather than mere rank. The point is that the hidden wisdom of the appointment became visible through knowledge used at its proper time.

The final clause reaches further than the angels' doubt, and that reach is the reason the verse sits at the heart of the passage. It is not only the open question that was known; what each creature keeps hidden is known as well. The Book makes this a standing theme, and the same words appear later when the listener is told plainly what the heart conceals: (2:284 — **“Whether you reveal what is in your hearts or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it.”**). The scene among the angels is therefore a small illustration of a general fact, and the reader who has followed the story is being asked to apply the fact to himself before the chapter moves on.

**A LESSON DRAWN AFTER THE DEMONSTRATION**

The order of the scene is deliberate and it repeats throughout the Book. God does not settle the matter by announcing the verdict; he lets the test run, so that nobody is asked to accept a judgement he has not seen. This is part of how the Qur'an argues. The idols are challenged to speak, the false claimants are challenged to produce, and here the critics are invited to examine what a creature has been given. Then the conclusion is drawn in the presence of the ones who raised the question. A reader can take confidence from the method itself, because it means the Book is willing to be examined while it makes its claims rather than after the fact. The other side of the method is that the answer arrives with a reminder of what people hide. The angels had one question, and the closing words of the verse widen the frame to everything that is kept back: the error covered over, the motive smoothed out of an account, the private arrangement that no audience ever sees. The Book returns to this widening move often because it is where the reader lives. He can follow a story about angels without difficulty; being told that his own concealed matters are known is a different exercise altogether. The verse puts both in one breath, and the chapter expects the reader to carry the two together from here onward.

**THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN KNOWING AND BEING KNOWN**

A reader can draw one practical distinction from the passage and carry it through the week. He knows a small amount, he can be wrong about most of it, and he is fully known. Those three facts arrange a life differently from the way most people arrange theirs. The first keeps him learning, the second keeps him humble, and the third keeps him honest when nobody is checking. The angels in the scene model the first two, and the last clause of the verse is aimed at the third, which is the one the reader controls. For a reader, the work is straightforward. Take one thing that has been kept concealed, whether from people or from an account a person gives about himself, and deal with it before the Lord who already knows it. The verse does not suggest that everything must be said publicly; the Book is not asking its reader to broadcast his faults. It is asking him to stop arranging his life as though the concealment were real, and to act on the fact that the one who taught Adam the names also knows what each of his descendants keeps back. A sealed examination paper is opened only after the student has answered, and the result then proves what the examiner already knew. The scene works in that way, except that the divine knowledge also reaches the motive hidden behind every answer. This week, a hidden account still stands before the One who knows it, because delay changes no part of what is known.

---

## Verse 2:34

> And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful

**ORDER RECEIVED AND REFUSAL EXPOSED**

The scene closes with an order and its consequences: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,””***, ***“so they all did”***, ***“but not Iblîs, who refused”***, ***“and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful”***. The sentence reports obedience in four words and then spends the rest of its length on the exception, which tells the reader where the danger lies. Think of a household where everyone answers a call but one, and the one who declines becomes the whole story of the evening. That distribution is the teaching. The angels' response is mentioned because it is the norm, and the refusal is detailed because it is the danger the reader needs to see clearly. The Book does not leave the reader to guess what went wrong or where: the two words that describe it are pride and unbelief, and they are named in the order in which they occurred. A reading carried from Ibn ʿAbbās places Iblīs among the worshippers before this refusal exposed him. That history matters because the former labour did not protect a heart that placed its own worth above a present command.

The command to prostrate has been the subject of long discussion among the teachers, and the point they agree on is that it was an act of honour by command rather than worship of the creature. The prostration of the angels is a sign of obedience to their Lord, and the one who refused was not objecting to the honour of Adam so much as to the right of the commander to command him. The Book reports his reasoning in other places and lets him condemn himself out of his own mouth: (7:12 — **“Allah asked, “What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?” He replied, “I am better than he is:”**), with the difference in material serving as his whole argument. The reader who hears that reasoning has heard the voice of every pride that ever dressed itself up as principle.

**WHY PRIDE ENDS IN DISBELIEF**

The verse puts arrogance first and unbelief second, and the order is not accidental. Nothing in the story suggests that Iblîs began by denying his Lord's existence; he began by declining to obey because he thought himself better placed to judge. That is the route the Book warns about in every generation, and it is the reason so many of its warnings are aimed at the proud rather than at the ignorant, since an ignorant person may still be taught while a proud one has stopped listening. A person who will not accept a command from someone he considers beneath him has already placed his own judgement above the one who gave it, whether or not he would ever say such a thing aloud.

The refusal is reported in several sūrahs with the same core and different details, and together they show a hardened path rather than a single bad moment. In one, the command is repeated and the objection is extended: (17:61 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who protested,”**), and in another the refusal is described with the same adverb of contempt: (20:116 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused ˹arrogantly˺”**). The repetition is not redundancy. It is the Book pressing on a point the reader is most likely to misapply to someone else.

**THE TEST THAT HAS NOT CHANGED**

The test in this verse is uncomfortable because it is not primarily about a strange creature in an ancient scene. It is about a person who is asked to do something he considers beneath him, or to honour someone he considers inferior, or to accept a ruling that does not flatter his estimate of himself. The reader meets that test in his household, in his work, and in the smallest obligations of his religion, and the pattern of his answers is the pattern of his loyalty. The angels passed the test without discussion, and their obedience took four words to report. What the reader does with the same test will take a lifetime to report. In practice, a reader should look for the one thing he resists not because it is unclear but because yielding would cost him a little pride. Naming it honestly is most of the work, since the resistance usually comes with a respectable reason attached. The Book is not interested in the reason; it is interested in whether the prostration happens. A person who can bow in that one place has understood the scene, and one who cannot has repeated the refusal in a smaller setting with the same result. The way a fine uniform cannot excuse a guard who rejects a direct order, long worship could not excuse this refusal. The test exposed who regarded obedience as service and who regarded service as proof of personal rank. In a workplace today, pride can reject a sound instruction merely because it came through someone of lower rank.

---

## Verse 2:35

> We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”

**THE HOUSE WITH ONE TREE FENCED OFF**

The story turns to the first household and to its single restriction: ***“We cautioned, “O Adam!”***, ***“Live with your wife in Paradise”***, ***“and eat as freely”***, ***“as you please, but do not approach this tree”***, ***“or else you will be wrongdoers.””***. The permission comes before the prohibition, and its breadth is part of the scene. Every tree in the garden is available, the food is free, and the instruction to settle and enjoy is given without a condition. Against that background stands one tree, and the wording does not say "do not eat from it" but "do not approach it", which fences off the road as well as the fruit. A boundary drawn that carefully is a kindness rather than a tease, because it keeps a person away from the road that leads to the line. The Book gives the same instruction in the same terms elsewhere, and the phrasing there makes the limit a matter of approach rather than of appetite. Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās place Adam and his wife together under this one limit. Their shared residence therefore included shared duty, which means neither abundance nor companionship removed the need to obey the boundary set by their Lord.

The Book uses this same scene in other sūrahs, and the details given there show how the test was meant to work. In one account the warning is paired with the identity of the one who would try to undo it: (7:20 — **“Then Satan tempted them in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said,”**), and in another the temptation is quoted as an offer of something more than they had: (20:120 — **“But Satan whispered to him, saying, “O Adam! Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality”**). The reader who puts the passages together sees the design plainly. A generous provision, a narrow limit, and an enemy whose whole work is to make the limit look like deprivation.

**WHY ONE TREE WAS ENOUGH**

A reader may wonder why a garden full of permission needed a prohibition at all. The answer the passage gives is that a creature with real choice needs a place to exercise it, and a limit is where love becomes visible as obedience, since obedience without a boundary would be a word without a test. The instruction was not given because the fruit was harmful in itself; it was given so that the relationship had a shape a person could keep or break. That is what makes the disaster in the next verse comprehensible, since the wrong in the story was not a poisoned meal. It was the decision to treat one clear boundary as though it were a negotiable detail. The verse names the consequence in advance, and it does so in the language of the law rather than the language of sentiment: whoever crosses the line is a wrongdoer. Nothing in the sentence suggests that the penalty would fall immediately, and nothing suggests it would be forgotten. The Book treats the warning as complete and leaves the choice to the two people standing in front of it. Everything that follows in the story is the outworking of a decision made by creatures who had been told exactly what it would cost.

**THE LIMITS A READER KEEPS AT ARM'S LENGTH**

The practical value of the verse is that it forces a comparison a reader may not want to make. Every life has a wide field of permitted things and a small number of boundaries drawn tightly around them, and the boundaries are usually the ones a person spends his attention on. That is precisely the inversion the scene warns against. The garden was given for enjoyment, and the two people in it lost the whole of it over the one thing they were told to leave alone. The Book does not present the limit as a burden; it presents the limit as the place where a person's answer to his Lord becomes visible. Today the useful exercise is to name one boundary that has been kept at arm's length, in the hope that a technical distance would count as obedience. The wording of the verse closes that gap in advance: what is forbidden is the approach, not only the act. A reader who accepts the fence where it stands has learned the lesson the two residents of the garden learned too late, and he has learned it while the trees on his side of the fence are still his to enjoy. Think of a wide orchard with one fenced corner: abundance makes the fence easier to honour, not harder to understand. The single limit exposed whether the gift would be received on the Giver's terms or turned into a claim of ownership.

---

## Verse 2:36

> But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”

**THE SLIP AND THE SENTENCE THAT FOLLOWED IT**

The tree was approached and the household fell: ***“But Satan deceived them”***, ***“leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in”***, ***“and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺”***, ***“as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence”***, ***“and provision for your appointed stay.””***. The Book does not describe a long campaign or a gradual seduction; it says the deception worked and the two were out. Then comes the sentence of removal, and inside it the reader finds something he did not expect, which is provision. The same order that expels them names the earth as a place to live, food to eat, and a term to serve, and all three are given by the one who is sending them down. Qatādah described Satan's act as a tripping that removed the pair from their former state. The image matters because a trip begins at one point yet changes the traveler's whole position, so the warning concerns the first yielding as much as the fall that follows.

The details of the temptation are reported in full elsewhere, and they show why the slip was so easy to arrange. In one account the tempter's approach is described as a promise of a different kind of life: (7:20 — **“Then Satan tempted them in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said,”**), and the speech that follows offers no argument but a comparison. The Book reports the same technique in the sūrah of Ṭā-Hā with a whisper about immortality and a kingdom that never ends: (20:120 — **“But Satan whispered to him, saying, “O Adam! Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality”**). Neither account shows a reasoned case against the command. Both show an appetite being widened, which is how the thing still works.

**ENMITY STATED IN ADVANCE**

The sentence of descent includes a fact that shapes everything after it: the two parties would be enemies to each other, and the earth would be the ground on which that enmity plays out. The reader is being told, at the beginning of the human story, that he has an opponent and that the opponent is not going to change his method. What makes the passage steadying rather than frightening is the rest of the same sentence. The opponent was granted no control over the residence or the provision; those come from someone else. The Book repeats the scene in another sūrah where the same promise of guidance follows the descent immediately: (20:123 — **“Allah said, “Descend, both of you, from here together ˹with Satan˺ as enemies to each other.”**), and the next words there describe guidance arriving for whoever follows it. The word for the stay is the word for a fixed term, which is the one detail a person is most tempted to forget. A residence with a term is not a homeland, and provision for a term is not an inheritance. The Book elsewhere states the whole arrangement in three clauses and leaves nothing vague: (7:25 — **“He added, “There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be resurrected.””**). The reader who holds those clauses together has the shape of his own life in his hands, and the shape changes the way he treats the ground under him, since a term makes a person careful about what he builds.

**THE MECHANICS OF LOSING GROUND**

The practical weight of the verse is that the fall did not come from a lack of information. Adam and his wife knew the command, knew the limit, and knew the warning that came with it. What they lacked was the willingness to keep a boundary while a desire was being widened on the other side of it. That is a description the reader can test in his own case without difficulty, because he also keeps a short list of limits that he knows and does not always keep. The story is not told to make a person despair of himself; it is told so that he recognises the mechanics by which he loses ground, and recognises them before the loss.
