The work for a reader now is to name the one place where the pattern operates and to put something in its way, since the verse shows that a limit without a guard usually does not hold. The Book does not pretend that a person stops slipping after he has been warned once. It shows him the slip that cost the first household everything, tells him the enemy is still at work, and then promises guidance to whoever follows it, which means the story of this verse is the beginning of a road rather than the end of one. It is like a tenant who ignores one term of a generous lease and loses the room that made the breach seem small. The size of the forbidden act cannot be measured apart from the authority of the One whose limit was crossed. These days, a small private compromise can shift an entire household because the first breach redraws what later feels normal.

---

## Verse 2:37

> Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**WORDS GIVEN TO A MAN WHO HAD JUST FALLEN**

The story does not end with the descent, because the next verse says what happened between the fall and the sentence: ***“Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord,”***, and ***“so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”***. The words were not invented by the man; they were placed in him, which is the difference between a creature left to improvise his way back and a creature who is handed the door. The Book reports the prayer itself in another sūrah, and the wording there shows what the inspired words were: (7:23 — **“They replied, “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us,”**). The confession is complete, and it contains no excuse and no attempt to share the blame. Two things are joined in that sentence: the admission that the wrong was their own, and the appeal for mercy rather than for justice. A person who has understood the story of the fall will notice how much those two clauses cover. Adam does not blame the serpent, and he does not blame his wife, and he does not blame the intensity of the desire that was stirred in him. He names himself as the one who did the wrong and then asks for something he has no claim on. That is what the verse calls a return, and the Book treats it as the model for everyone who comes after him. Mujāhid identified the received words with the confession preserved in the sūrah of the Heights. This transmitted reading joins the two passages directly, which means Adam's return rested on an honest admission and a plea for mercy rather than on a defence of his conduct.

**THE SHAPE OF AN ACCEPTED RETURN**

The answer arrives immediately and it is described in two names, and both of them matter to a reader who is afraid that his own record disqualifies him. The one who accepts the return is called the Accepter of Repentance and the Most Merciful, and the Book repeats these descriptions wherever it wants a person to stop despairing of himself. The same acceptance is reported in another sūrah with a third element joined to the other two: (20:122 — **“Then his Lord chose him ˹for His grace˺, accepted his repentance, and guided him ˹rightly˺”**). Chosen, accepted, and guided: the verse supplies more than forgiveness, because it supplies the road afterwards. The contrast with the previous scene is the sharpest thing in the passage. One creature refused a command, and another creature broke one, and the difference in what happened to them is not explained by the size of the offense. It is explained by what each did when the moment came. One argued about his own worth, and the other admitted a fault and asked for mercy, and the Book lets the reader draw the conclusion without a sentence of commentary. A person who reads both scenes on the same page has received one of the plainest lessons the Qur'an offers about how to fail.

**WHAT RETURNING REQUIRES OF A READER**

Two things follow from the line: a person can always come back, and he cannot come back on his own terms. The words were given, which means the returning has a shape the Lord has set rather than one the returning person prefers. The Book elsewhere describes the same road with more detail: (20:82 — **“But I am truly Most Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does good, then persists on ˹true˺ guidance.””**). Repentance, belief, good conduct, and persistence: the four items are not four separate tasks so much as four faces of one direction, and a person who takes the direction will find every one of them changing the others. The exercise for a reader is to say the sentence the inspired words contain, in the plainest way available, about the thing a reader has been excusing to himself for years. The excuse is the part that has to go, because the excuse is what keeps the fault in place and the person comfortable. The Book holds out an immediate acceptance in the same verse as the fall, and a reader who delays his return while waiting to feel worthy has misunderstood both halves of the sentence. Picture a child who breaks something and is then taught the exact words of an honest apology. The gift of those words does not erase responsibility; it opens a sound road back when shame might otherwise keep the child hiding. Today, excuses travel quickly, but the received prayer remains short because return begins when blame is no longer moved elsewhere.

---

## Verse 2:38

> We said, “Descend all of you! Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**A PROMISE MADE TO EVERYONE LEAVING THE GARDEN**

The descent is spoken again, and this time it carries an undertaking: ***“We said, “Descend all of you!”***, ***“Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear”***, ***“for them, nor will they grieve”***. The repetition of the departure is not idle, because the second telling is addressed to a crowd rather than to a household. The collective command reaches everyone who would ever be born into the world below. Into that address the Lord places a promise: guidance will come, and the promise is made before anyone has asked for it. The Book is describing a road that has been supplied with signs before its travellers set out. The last clause then defines what is being offered in the only terms a person can verify. No fear and no grief: one looks forward and the other looks back, and between the two of them lies the whole of a person's unease. What follows guidance in this sentence is not prosperity or safety or length of days. It is the removal of the two weights that make the present unbearable and the past unforgettable, and the Book treats those two removals as the substance of the promise rather than as its decoration. A reader who has carried either weight understands immediately how much is being offered. Abū al-ʿĀliyah understood the promised guidance to include messengers, clear signs and plain teaching. Ibn ʿAbbās also tied following it to safety from error and misery. The reading gives the promise a public form, because people are not left to search for a private signal when God sends words that can be learned and followed.

**A PROMISE RESTATED AFTER THE DESCENT**

The Book repeats the sentence in several places, and each time the repetition anchors the reader a little more. In the sūrah of the Heights the condition is described with a moral clause attached: (7:35 — **“O children of Adam! When messengers from among yourselves come to you reciting My revelations—whoever”**), and the promise closes the same way there, with no fear and no grief for the ones who mend their ways. Even the children of Israel are given the same terms in this very sūrah when their own account is described: (2:62 — **“Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and”**), and the ending of that verse repeats the two negations word for word. The wording stays constant because the offer does not change with the audience. The guidance in the promise is not a private intuition. The Book consistently attaches it to messengers and to a revealed scripture, which is why the promise appears in practical terms in the sūrah of Ṭā-Hā: (20:123 — **“Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray ˹in this life˺”**). The pattern is the same everywhere. A message arrives, a person follows it, and the fear and the grief lose their grip. Nothing in the arrangement depends on a person's ancestry, his language, or his position, which gives the collective address its wide mercy in a story about an expelled household.

**A WEEK WITHOUT THE TWO WEIGHTS**

A reader who wants to put this sentence to work can ask what his week would look like if the two weights were actually gone. The fear of what may come is usually carried in the form of hoarding and hustling, and the grief over what has passed is usually carried as resentment or as a story told about oneself. Both of them occupy a great deal of room, and both of them are named in the promise as things a follower of guidance does not have to keep. The Book does not ask a person to pretend that the losses did not happen. It asks him to follow the guidance, and it says the following is what makes the difference. A reader can begin by tracing one recurring fear and one recurring grief back to a decision made without reference to the guidance that has arrived. That tracing is not an accusation, and the verse does not present it as one. It presents the promise first, in the sentence spoken as the household left the garden, and it leaves the reader to notice that the offer has been standing ever since. The way a marked road carries a traveller through country he has never seen, revealed guidance carries the children of Adam through a world outside their first home. The safety lies in following the marks rather than inventing a path after every turn. In this age, abundant advice does not replace revealed direction, because more voices can still leave a traveller without a true road.

---

## Verse 2:39

> But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**THE OTHER END OF THE SAME SENTENCE**

The promise has a counterpart, and the sūrah states it without softening: ***“But those who disbelieve”***, and ***“and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.””***. Two conditions are named, and the order matters. The first is a refusal, and the second is what refusal becomes once it has something concrete to reject. The Book does not describe the people in this line as uninformed; the signs are named as things they have denied, which means the signs were there to be met. The sentence is the closing bracket of the opening scene of the chapter, and it lands with the same finality as the promise that precedes it. The word for residence in this verse is the same word the sūrah used for the wrongdoers in the garden, and it is also the word used in this chapter for the people who are settled in their unbelief. The Book likes to keep that thread visible, because it wants the reader to see that the two destinies in the opening verses are not a pair of moods but a pair of tenancies. One group is promised that fear and grief will be lifted from them; the other is told what their permanent address will be. Nothing in the arrangement is hidden, and nothing about it is negotiable after the fact. Ibn ʿAbbās linked following the promised guidance with safety from misery in the next life. The opposite course therefore reaches the opposite home, and another verse states the outcome in the same settled terms: (3:116 — **“who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever”**).

**OPENING CASE REACHES ITS TWO ENDS**

The order of the sūrah's opening chapters of thought is worth tracing, because the reader has now passed through all of it. First the Book was described as a guide for the mindful. Then the readers were divided into the guided, the sealed, and the double-minded. Then the whole of humanity was called to worship, challenged to produce a sūrah, warned about the fire, and given good news about the gardens. Then the story of Adam and Iblīs supplied the mechanism behind all of it: a command, a choice, a fall, and a return. Now the two endings are stated one after the other, and the reader has been given every piece of information he needs to understand what the choice involves. The Book is not unusual among scriptures in naming a punishment, and it is unusual in the amount of reasoning it places in front of the warning. A person reading this chapter has been argued with, reminded, shown his own biography, told about his enemy, and given the terms of forgiveness before the fire is mentioned a second time. That sequence is the answer to anyone who says the Book threatens first and explains later. The explained version is exactly what the sūrah has been building from its opening line, and the two verses about the residents of each destination are simply where the argument lands.

**DENYING SIGNS IN AN ORDINARY WEEK**

The phrase about denying signs can sound far away from a reader who has never formally rejected a scripture, and the Book uses it in a way that brings it home. A sign is anything that points beyond itself, and a person denies signs whenever he explains away what he has plainly seen: the answered prayer he attributes to coincidence, the limit he crosses while telling himself the matter is not settled, the verse he avoids because it has asked him for something. None of that is dramatic, and none of it looks like unbelief at the time, which is precisely why it is dangerous. The verse names the endpoint rather than each step toward it, and the reader is expected to supply the steps from his own week. Today the honest exercise is to take one sign that has been explained away and to stop explaining it. The verse does not ask anyone to feel certain about what comes after death; it asks him not to deny what he has already been shown. A person who can do that much has separated himself from the group described in this line, and he has done it at the only moment available to anyone, which is the one he is living in now. Imagine two leases whose terms and endings are printed before either key is accepted. The warning removes any claim of surprise, because denial is shown with its destination while faith is shown with its freedom from fear and grief.

---

## Verse 2:40

> O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine, and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺

**THE ADDRESS TURNS TO A NEW AUDIENCE**

The story of Adam closes and the sūrah turns to a people who will occupy most of its remaining pages: ***“O children of Israel!”***, ***“Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant”***, ***“and I will fulfil Mine”***, ***“and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺”***. The change of address is abrupt and deliberate. After describing the first household and the promise made to everyone leaving the garden, the Book speaks directly to the community that had inherited a scripture, a history, and a set of obligations, and it speaks to them with the same word it has used throughout the chapter: remember. A long account now shows what that community did with its inheritance, and this verse stands at the door of the account with an invitation rather than an accusation. The favours named in the sentence are not itemised here, and the reader is expected to know what they were. The Book spells them out later in the chapter with a list that runs from the rescue at the sea to the shade in the desert and the manna from the sky, and each item is introduced with the same command to recall. The word for favour names a benefit freely given, which means the remembering is not about flattery. A person who has been carried for generations is being asked to notice by whom, and the notice is the first step of gratitude. Everything else in the passage follows from whether that step happens. Mujāhid counted among these favours the rescue from Pharaoh, the water brought from stone, and the food sent in the wilderness. The command to remember is therefore tied to known events, because a covenant rests on gifts that the community could name from its own inherited account.

**HOW A COVENANT IS PRESENTED**

The middle of the verse sets out a transaction, and the Book does not disguise its shape. The command to fulfil the human side stands beside the divine promise of fulfilment, yet the relationship never becomes a bargain between two equals. Even the phrasing shows the asymmetry, since the command falls on the human party while the promise of fulfilment is spoken by the Lord who did not need the covenant in the first place. The Book gives the same covenant a detailed form later in the chapter: (2:63 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you”**), and it summarises the terms at the beginning of another passage: (5:12 — **“Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel and appointed twelve leaders from among them and ˹then˺ said,”**). The pattern is consistent. The covenant is an arrangement of grace in which the initiative belongs to one side and the obligation to the other. The verse then ends with a command that fits the arrangement: stand in awe of Me alone. The word is the same one the sūrah opened with when it described the mindful, which brings the chapter back to its opening description with more information now in view. Awe of one is the practical form of loyalty to one, and it is offered here as the single alternative to the kind of divided attention the earlier verses described so carefully. The children of Israel are not accused yet. They are told what their position requires of them.

**AN INHERITANCE THAT CAN STILL BE HONOURED**

For a reader who is not a child of Israel, the question raised here is the question of inheritance, since every reader receives something from the generations before him. A tradition, a language, a set of habits, a community that carried him when he could not carry himself, and a revealed book that reached him through other people's labour: the list of favours in the sentence is longer in his own case than he assumes. The verse asks two things of whoever holds such an inheritance, remembrance and fulfilment, and both are within reach today. Remembering requires the naming of what was given, and fulfilment requires one concrete act of loyalty to the terms attached to it. The exercise is to write down three gifts received from the generations before him and, beside each, one obligation that comes with it. What is wanted is the response the gift has always required rather than a warm feeling about the past. A person who honours one such obligation has answered this verse in the way the children of Israel were being invited to answer it, with a deed rather than a sentiment, and the chapter's later verses will show what happens to a community that chooses the sentiment alone. It is like an heir receiving both a house and the duty to keep its trust, a community receives favour together with covenant. Memory keeps the gift from looking self-made, and awe keeps the inherited position from becoming a claim against its Giver. The point is that covenant memory must produce a fitting act, because a favour recalled without its duty becomes a title used against the purpose of the gift.

---

## Verse 2:41

> Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures. Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain. And be mindful of Me

**THE BOOK THAT ARRIVES CONFIRMING AN EARLIER ONE**

The address to the children of Israel continues with a demand and a description of the thing being demanded: ***“Believe in My revelations”***, ***“which confirm your Scriptures. Do not be the first to deny them”***, ***“or trade them for a fleeting gain.”***, and ***“And be mindful of Me”***. The order of the clauses is the argument of the verse. The new revelation is presented as a confirmation of what the audience already had, which means the invitation is not to leave their inheritance but to recognise it. Then comes the warning about being first in denial, which places a particular weight on the people who hold the keys to a tradition. Then the motive is named in four words, and the motive is money. Ibn ʿAbbās read the warning about being first as a charge against people whose knowledge gave them an earlier duty to respond. Their place mattered because refusal from a recognised guide could make later refusal easier for everyone who trusted that guide.

The Book repeats the confirmation argument in several places, and one statement of it is unusually direct about the recognition involved: (2:146 — **“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children.”**). A person does not mistake his own child. The verse is claiming that the men it addresses are not working from ignorance but from knowledge they have decided not to act on, and it treats the refusal as a decision with a price attached: the fleeting gain of the second clause. The Book elsewhere reports the same community bargaining in the same currency: (2:89 — **“when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺,”**), with the rejection following in the same sentence.

**THE PRICE PAID IN SMALL COIN**

The description of the price is the part of the verse that travels furthest. What the men being addressed stood to lose was status, an income, and the deference of a community that looked to them for rulings, and it was all temporary in the plainest sense of the word. Every generation has the same exchange on offer, and it rarely presents itself as betrayal. It appears as a career, a reputation, a place at the table, a family arrangement that cannot be disturbed. The Book calls the sum fleeting rather than forbidden, which is a sharper way of putting it, since a person can imagine giving up something large but not something that will vanish anyway. The last clause returns the reader to the single relationship that decides how all of this is weighed: be mindful of Me. The word is the same one that appeared at the beginning of the chapter and again at the start of this address, and its repetition is a clue that the sūrah is circling one theme. The men in view are not being asked to abandon their heritage or their scriptures. They are being asked to stop managing the truth for a price, and the only motive strong enough to compete with the price is the awareness that the transaction is being observed.

**THE MINUTE AFTER RECOGNITION**

Every reader has met the moment when he recognises something true and immediately begins calculating what accepting it would cost. The calculation is almost never conscious; it shows up as a delay, a request for more evidence, or an interest in the character of the person who said it. The Book names that moment here and calls the calculation a trade, and it does so in the middle of a long passage about people who had a genuine inheritance in their hands. The reader is meant to see that possession of the truth is not the test. The test is what he does in the minute after he recognises it. The exercise is to name one thing he has recognised and postponed, and to write down the price he is being offered to keep postponing it. Naming the figure usually removes its charm, because the figure is almost always small: a conversation avoided, an apology delayed, a change of habit put off a year. The verse ends with the two words that make the delay unreasonable, and they are not addressed to a community but to a person, since the command to be mindful of God has never been issued to a crowd without reaching each member of it. A merchant who exchanges a lasting title for the coins in one day's till has mistaken what can be spent for what should be kept. The verse measures every gain by its duration, so a benefit that dies with a position is small even when it fills the hand today.

---

## Verse 2:42

> Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly

**TWO DIFFERENT CRIMES AGAINST THE TRUTH**

The next sentence names the failure in its two practical forms: ***“Do not mix truth with falsehood”***, and ***“or hide the truth knowingly”***. The two are distinct, and the sūrah deals with them as a pair, because a person who is willing to do one of them will usually end up doing the other before long. Mixing is the active work of blending, where a true statement is wrapped around a false one until the listener cannot separate them. Hiding is the quieter work of omission, where the relevant material is simply left out of the account. Both produce the same result in the hearer, and both are named as deliberate acts rather than as mistakes of memory or understanding. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the first offence as mixing established facts with lies, while Qatādah treated the mixture as a deliberate joining of rival claims. Both readings make knowledge central, which means the sin lies in managing the truth rather than simply failing to find it.

The Book raises the same charge against the same community in another sūrah, and the wording there puts a question mark where this verse puts a command: (3:71 — **“O People of the Book! Why do you mix the truth with falsehood and hide the truth knowingly”**). The pairing is identical, which suggests that the Book regards the two as one habit seen from two sides. The people being addressed had a scripture in their hands and an audience that trusted them, and the temptation ran in both directions at once: to present a case by blending, and to protect a position by silence. A reader who has ever made an argument for a good cause will recognise the first of those, and one who has ever let a wrong stand because correcting it would be awkward will recognise the second.

**THE ADVERB THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING**

Everything in the verse turns on the adverb. The Book does not accuse anyone of an honest error, and it does not treat confusion as a crime. What it names is the deliberate management of information by people who know what they are doing, and that is why the sentence can be so short and still land so heavily. The Book elsewhere describes the opposite conduct as the obligation of the same community, and it is expressed in one clause: (3:187 — **“who were given the Scripture to make it known to people and not hide it,”**). The covenant required publication, and the practice described in this verse is the covenant reversed. The word also protects the reader from two errors of self-assessment. A person who has been wrong through carelessness can correct himself and move on, since the Book is full of that story. A person who has been hiding something knowingly is in a different position, because his problem is not information but willingness. The verse asks him to stop, and it does not pretend that the stopping is difficult to identify. He already knows the material he has been leaving out, which is the reason the adverb is there in the first place.

**HANDLING MATERIAL HONESTLY**

The practical instruction is about the handling of material, and it applies far beyond the study of scripture. A person who quotes a report and leaves out the sentence that changes its meaning has mixed. A person who is asked for advice and omits the one fact that would have altered the decision has hidden. Both can be done with an entirely clear conscience, which is why the Book keeps the command in front of the reader in the plainest possible form. It is not asking him to be clever about the truth. It is asking him not to arrange it. The exercise is to find one place where an account he gives has been trimmed for convenience, and to restore the missing piece the next time the matter comes up. Nothing about the verse requires him to be brutal or to volunteer information that no one has asked for. It requires him to stop being the editor of the truth when he is the one who benefits from the editing. A person who can do that in one recurring conversation has begun the work that this verse and the one before it are asking for. Think of clear water mixed with a little dye: the vessel may still look useful, yet every cup now carries the added colour. Truth arranged with falsehood works the same way, since the false part changes how the true part is received. A public claim today can be distorted by one withheld fact, which means this command governs headlines, meetings and family accounts alike.

---

## Verse 2:43

> Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down

**THREE ACTS THAT PUT A PERSON IN A ROW**

The address closes its first movement with an instruction that is entirely practical: ***“Establish prayer, pay alms-tax”***, ***“and bow down with those”***, ***“who bow down”***. Two of the three acts are private in their motive and public in their effect, and the third is unmistakably social. Bowing with those who bow is the clause that gathers the other two into a community, and it is placed last so that the sentence ends on the visible sign. A person can pray alone in a room and give quietly from a distance, and the Book praises both. But the verse does not stop there, and the reason is that a religion practised only in private quickly becomes a religion shaped by private preferences. Qatādah named prayer and alms here as two binding duties that must be rendered to God. The transmitted reading keeps the commands concrete, because the public bow does not replace the personal duty and the personal gift does not replace worship with the congregation.

The pairing of prayer and alms is one of the most frequent combinations in the Book, and its repetition shows how tightly the two are bound. In this sūrah the pair is repeated almost word for word when the same community is addressed again: (2:110 — **“Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves,”**), with the promise attached that the good will be found with God. The sūrah of the Clear Proof states the same two obligations for the people of an earlier scripture and calls them the upright way: (98:5 — **“and pay alms-tax. That is the upright Way”**). The reader is being taught one pattern from several angles: the worship that faces God and the charity that faces people are not two separate duties but one life turned in a single direction.

**THE CLAUSE THAT PUTS A PERSON IN A ROW**

The final clause is the one that would have cost the original audience the most, because bowing with the congregation meant being counted among the followers of the new prophet. The men being addressed held a position in their own community, and the command asked them to line up in a row behind someone else. That is why the phrase is not a decorative addition to the other two. It is the public test of whether the private devotions were sincere, and the Book uses community and visible practice as its ordinary way of testing the inner claim. A person who has believed something and will not stand in a row with the people who believe it has a private opinion rather than a religion.

The Book elsewhere shows what the same three acts look like when they take hold of a community rather than an individual: (22:41 — **“˹They are˺ those who, if established in the land by Us, would perform prayer, pay alms-tax, encourage what is good,”**). Prayer, charity, and the ordering of public life are named there in one breath, which is the shape the Book expects the obligations to take when they are lived out by a group. The verse in this sūrah begins with two of them and ends with the congregation, and the later verse shows where the congregation is meant to lead. The pattern is not a coincidence of wording; it is a description of a way of living.

**THE ROW A PERSON JOINS**

What the verse requires is that the reader be findable by the people he claims to belong to. A person whose religion leaves no trace that anyone can check has arranged a version of the faith that cannot be tested by anyone but himself, and the Book has already explained in this chapter where that arrangement usually leads. Bowing with those who bow is a small act with a large consequence: it puts a person's name next to other names, subject to the same timetable, the same leader, and the same obligations. What is wanted here is a place in the row, not a public display of the private life. The exercise is to attend one congregational prayer that has been skipped for convenience, and to go early enough to bow with the others rather than arriving at the end. The Book is asking for a habit rather than an occasional gesture, and the habit is the one this verse names in its final clause. A reader who keeps it for a month will find that the two earlier obligations have also changed, since a person who bows in a row is much harder to satisfy with private arrangements. A prayer row is like a line of workers lifting one beam: each person bears his own weight, yet the shared line keeps the task straight. Worship, giving and public bowing place private loyalty inside a community that can see and support it. This week, one place kept in the prayer row can turn a private claim into a visible bond with the worshipping community.

---

## Verse 2:44

> Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture? Do you not understand

**THE TEACHERS WHO DO NOT DO WHAT THEY TEACH**

The second half of the address turns on the men themselves, and the questions come in a pair: ***“Do you preach righteousness”***, ***“and fail to practice it yourselves”***, ***“although you read the Scripture?”***, ***“Do you not understand”***. Nothing in the sentence disputes their learning; the reading is granted in the middle of the accusation. What is being questioned is the gap between the lesson and the life of the one delivering it, and the closing question asks whether such a person has understood the first thing about the book he carries, which he has presumably read more than once. The Book names this failure without any softening. It puts the charge in the mouth of the Lord and lets it stand without a defence. Qatādah described people who ordered obedience while contradicting their own orders, and al-Suddī carried the same reading. The fault therefore lies not in teaching righteousness but in granting the teacher an exemption, which is why the verse challenges understanding rather than knowledge alone.

The same rebuke is given to the community in another sūrah in a single line, and the brevity there is what makes it unforgettable: (61:3 — **“How despicable it is in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do”**). The Book elsewhere shows what a teacher is supposed to be, and the alternative is stated as a role rather than a technique: (3:79 — **“Rather, he would say, “Be devoted to the worship of your Lord ˹alone˺”—in”**), with the rest of that verse explaining that the model of a scholar is a person whose teaching is visible in his own devotion. The contrast between the two passages is the whole moral: the Book honours the teacher and despises the performance.

**A CHARGE AIMED AT TEACHERS FIRST**

A reader might ask why the sūrah spends its sharpest words on the people who at least know the text. The answer is in the structure of the community. A teacher's practice sets the ceiling for everyone who learns from him, and a man who instructs others in a discipline he does not keep teaches two lessons at once, the second of which is that the discipline is optional. The Book treats that as a heavier offence than private negligence, because its damage is multiplied by every student the man has. That is why the address in this sūrah reaches the scholars before it reaches anyone else in the audience. There is also a mercy inside the rebuke. The verse does not tell the teachers to stop teaching; it asks them to stop being the exception to their own instruction, which means the correction can happen without a change of office. A person in that position is not asked to give up his place but to earn it in the only way the Book recognises, by doing what he says. The question comes at the end of the paragraph's case, and with its invitation to think it leaves the door open for exactly that. The Book keeps the door open even while it names the offence in the plainest possible terms.

**THE GAP A READER CAN MEASURE**

The line reaches every reader who has ever passed on advice, which is to say all of them. A parent instructs, a friend advises, a colleague corrects, and the same gap opens up wherever the instruction outruns the life. The measure the Book gives is not perfection, since nobody keeps his own advice completely. The measure is the direction of the gap: whether a person is moving toward the standard he describes or using his knowledge as a licence to remain where he is. A teacher who is visibly ashamed of his own shortfall teaches something valuable. A teacher who is untroubled by it has already been described by this verse. One practical step is to take a piece of advice given to someone in the last month and apply the same standard to himself this week. That act is the answer the verse is looking for, and it requires no audience. A person who does it quietly in one matter has put the question of this verse behind him, at least until the next time somebody asks him for guidance and he has to look in the mirror first. Picture a coach who gives exact instructions but never enters the training ground. His words may remain correct, yet his absence teaches that the standard belongs to others. The verse closes that second lesson by placing the teacher under the command he speaks.

---

## Verse 2:45

> And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—

**TWO THINGS TO CARRY INTO TROUBLE**

The address shifts from rebuke to help, and the help is described in two instruments: ***“And seek help through patience”***, ***“and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except”***, ***“for the humble”***. The command is addressed to the same people who have just been criticised, and it names the remedy for the gap they were shown. Patience in the Book's vocabulary is not passive endurance; it is the deliberate holding of oneself steady while a difficulty continues, and it is paired here with the act of turning to God. The two together cover what a person can do and what he cannot, and the verse presents them as the ordinary machinery of a religious life rather than as an emergency measure. The Book returns to the same pair in a command to the believers, and the wording there adds the assurance the reader needs to attempt it: (2:153 — **“O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient”**). The pairing recurs because the two halves answer different problems. Patience addresses the length of a trial, which is what wears a person down, and prayer addresses the isolation, which is what makes the length unbearable. In the Book's arrangement a person does not choose between managing his situation and asking for help. He does the first while he does the second. Mujāhid connected patience here with fasting and treated the burden as prayer, while Ibn ʿAbbās described the humble as people who trust what God has revealed. These readings meet because restraint, worship and belief support one another, so the remedy trains both the body and the heart.

**THE HEAVINESS AND WHO CAN CARRY IT**

The verse then admits that the practice is heavy, and it does so before naming the people for whom it is not. That is worth noticing, because the Book is often accused of selling a remedy without mentioning the weight. Here the weight is stated in the middle of the sentence: the two instruments are a burden except for the humble. The exception is not a special class of people with unusual abilities. The word describes a person who has accepted his position as a creature, and the burden does not lighten because he is strong but because he has stopped resisting the arrangement. A reader who has tried to keep a new habit knows exactly what the burden feels like: the first weeks are dull, the benefit is invisible, and the appetite for quitting is constant. The verse explains why some people carry it and others do not, and the explanation is not willpower. The person who has admitted that he needs the practice itself will keep doing it without getting anything visible from it, and the person who is still measuring himself against his own estimate of his importance will find the same schedule intolerable. That is the whole difference the verse names.

**PUTTING THE TWO INSTRUMENTS TO WORK**

The two instruments have to be attached to one named difficulty rather than carried as general principles. A reader can name the problem that has been wearing him down, decide what patience means in that exact situation, and then give the same situation a share of his prayer. The Book does not ask for a grandiose response, and it does not promise a quick removal of the difficulty. It promises that the two things put in place will hold, because the arrangement comes from the one who made the person who is carrying it. The other side of the instruction concerns company. The verse implies that the burden is lightest for those who have taken the humble position, and the Book elsewhere builds communities of people whose shared practice carries the individual through the weeks when his own enthusiasm fails. A reader who wants the two instruments to survive should use them in the presence of others who are using them, which is the same conclusion the previous verse reached about bowing in the row. The way a porter uses steady steps and a shoulder strap to carry a load, a believer uses patience and prayer together. One keeps the person from dropping the duty during its long strain, while the other fastens the heart to the source of help. For life today, this pairing corrects two common errors. Effort without prayer can make the struggling person trust only his own endurance, while prayer without patient duty can become a wish for escape. The verse binds the two so that neither error governs the response.

---

## Verse 2:46

> those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return

**CERTAINTY MAKES THE WEIGHT LIGHT**

The previous verse named the humble as the exception, and this one describes them: ***“those who are certain”***, ***“that they will meet their Lord”***, ***“and to Him they will return”***. Three clauses, and each of them explains a different part of the lightness described in the previous verse. The certainty is not optimism and it is not a mood; it is a settled expectation about an event, and the Book builds on it as the foundation of everything a person does with his hours. A man who expects to stand in front of his Lord cannot arrange his life as though the appointment were imaginary, while a man who has stopped expecting it will find every religious obligation heavier than it needs to be. Mujāhid treated the expectation in this verse as certainty, and al-Suddī likewise read it as sure knowledge. The language therefore does not praise a guess about the future. It describes an inward conviction firm enough to change how prayer and patience are carried in the present.

The second clause names the meeting, and the Book uses that word for the encounter that settles everything. It is not a vague survival after death; it is a presentation, which is why the verse can build an entire disposition on it. The third clause names the return, which is about direction rather than destination, and it tells the reader where the road he is already walking is going. The Book joins the same three ideas when it describes people whose good deeds are performed with a trembling heart because they know they are going back: (23:60 — **“and who do whatever ˹good˺ they do with their hearts fearful, ˹knowing˺ that they will return to their Lord—”**). That verse explains why the certainty does not produce complacency.

**HOW CERTAINTY MAKES HARD THINGS LIGHT**

The mechanism the verse describes is worth tracing, because a reader can test whether he has it. A person who is sure of a meeting prepares for it, and preparation converts discomfort into a task. Fasting becomes training rather than deprivation, charity becomes an investment rather than a loss, and an early prayer becomes an appointment kept rather than a duty discharged. The Book presents the change as a consequence of the expectation, not as a reward for it, which is why the humble in this verse find the burden light before they have received anything. They are lightened by what they are looking forward to rather than by what they have already been given. The Book also shows what happens when the expectation is present but weak, and the picture is not of a person who abandons his religion but of one who keeps it with a divided mind. Such a person does the acts and resents them, complies with the letter and negotiates over the spirit, and the Book's remedy for that condition is exactly what this verse describes. Certainty is not a feeling to be summoned; it is built by the same practice whose lightness depends on it, and the sūrah has already supplied the practice in the two instruments of patience and prayer.

**LIVE AS THOUGH THE MEETING IS ON THE CALENDAR**

Putting the meeting somewhere in the plan is what the verse is asking for. A reader who writes nothing in the calendar does not intend the appointment, and the Book is asking him to intend it in the ordinary way he intends everything else. That does not mean morbid reflection; it means the small adjustments a person makes when a date is fixed: what he prepares, what he stops doing, and whom he tells about it. The whole of the verse turns on those adjustments, because they are what separates certainty from opinion. One decision that is being made on the assumption that no meeting is coming should be remade on the assumption that one is. The Book does not ask the reader to feel certain on command, and it does not treat doubt as a disqualification. It asks him to act on the certainty he claims, and the acting is how the claim becomes a fact in his life. A person who does that in one matter will find the burden of the previous verse easier to carry the next morning. A fixed journey on a calendar changes spending and preparation before the day arrives. Certainty about the meeting works in the same manner, because the future appointment gives present worship a reason stronger than mood. For a worker today, the expected meeting changes hidden choices because no task is treated as unseen by the One who receives the return.

---

## Verse 2:47

> O Children of Israel! Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you and how I honoured you above the others

**FORMER FAVOURS RECALLED ONCE MORE**

The favours are recounted again, and the wording is almost identical to the address that opened the earlier passage: ***“O Children of Israel!”***, ***“Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you”***, ***“and how I honoured you above the others”***. The Book repeats an address on purpose, and a reader who notices the repetition learns something about how the sūrah is built. Between the two addresses the chapter has placed a block of warnings, an account of the covenant, and the reminder about the Day when no help will be available. The repetition is a hinge: the same community is brought back to the same starting point with more information than it had the first time. The phrase about honouring them above the others has been read in more than one way, and the reading that fits the sūrah best is the one the Book states elsewhere in the same terms: (44:32 — **“And indeed, We chose the Israelites knowingly above the others”**). The choosing is explained in other passages as a matter of prophets, scripture, and a period of leadership, and the reader is not being asked to conclude that the honour was permanent or unconditional, since the very next verses list what happened when the terms were neglected. The verse names a favour that was given, and it does so in a community's own history, which is why the next sentence will set out the terms that came with it. Abū al-ʿĀliyah explained the honour through the kingship, messengers and Scriptures granted to that community in its own age. Mujāhid and Qatādah also confined the preference to the peoples of that time, which means the favour is historical and accountable rather than a permanent licence detached from obedience.

**GIFTS NAMED BEFORE ANYTHING IS ASKED**

Every time the Book addresses this community, the favours come first. The pattern is deliberate, and it is the pattern of the whole sūrah: the gift is named, and then the obligation that fits the gift is named. A reader who skips to the commands will find them arbitrary, and a reader who reads the reminder first will find them proportionate. The Book is asking a people to remember what they were carried through, and it treats that memory as the motive strong enough to make obedience reasonable. The demand never arrives without a history attached to it. The Book keeps this order even where the tone hardens later in the chapter, which is a sign that the order is not a rhetorical device. Moses addresses his people in the same way when he reminds them of what they received, and the reminder there is also followed by the command: (5:20 — **“And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Remember Allah's favours upon you”**). The pattern holds across the sūrahs, and a reader who learns to expect it can read any of these passages with a better sense of what the Book thinks a person needs before he is asked for anything.

**GRATITUDE AS THE ENGINE OF OBEDIENCE**

For a reader from another community, the plainest lesson in the sūrah is this: obligation follows memory, and the memory has to be kept alive deliberately. Every person carries a list of favours he did not arrange, and the list is usually invisible because it is the ground he stands on. The verse does not ask the children of Israel to feel grateful; it asks them to remember, which is a discipline rather than a sentiment, and the remembering is done by naming the favours rather than by waiting for an emotion. The exercise is to write the list of favours in his own case and then read the obligations in this chapter against it, one at a time. The Book is asking, in every one of these addresses, whether the response matches the gift. A reader who finds that his obligations look small against his list has understood the point the sūrah keeps making, and he has understood it without needing to be a member of the community that received the original address. The way a family archive preserves both a deed and the duties attached to it, remembered favour preserves honour together with its terms. The record becomes harmful when the title is kept and the obligation is removed. This limit also protects the present community from reading another people's honour with contempt. A gift is tested by the duty it creates, so the proper response today is to ask what account follows every privilege rather than to boast about who received it first.

---

## Verse 2:48

> Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given

**THE DAY WHEN NOTHING CAN BE BORROWED**

The warning that follows the reminder is the starkest in the passage: ***“Guard yourselves against the Day on”***, ***“which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken”***, ***“and no help will be given”***. Four doors are closed in a single sentence, and each of them corresponds to a hope people actually carry. Nobody will be able to lean on a relative, nobody's patron will be able to speak for him, no payment will be accepted, and no ally will arrive in time to be of any use. The Day itself is not described here; what is described is what will be unavailable on it, which is a more effective way of making a person prepare. Al-Suddī read the opening denial to mean that one soul cannot suffice for another. The point is personal liability, because every substitute named afterwards is another attempt to move the account away from the person whose deeds created it.

The same warning is repeated later in the sūrah almost word for word, and the repetition brackets this stretch of the chapter: (2:123 — **“And guard yourselves against the Day”**), with the list of closed doors repeated after it. The Book gives the reason for the closures in another place, and the reason is not cruelty but the absence of any rival authority: (82:19 — **“˹It is˺ the Day no soul will be of ˹any˺ benefit to another whatsoever, for all authority on”**), where the sentence ends by stating that authority on that Day belongs to Allah entirely. Once every claim to authority has been returned to its owner, the networks by which people help one another no longer function, because they were only ever operating on borrowed authority. They were never independent in the first place.

**FOUR DOORS AND THE PRESENT ARRANGEMENTS**

The four refusals are also a description of the present, and a reader can see his own arrangements in them. Every system of help that people rely on is a temporary structure: family connections, professional networks, influence, and the exchange of favours. None of it is evil, and the Book does not ask anyone to despise it. It asks him to notice what it is for, and the verse is telling him that whatever it is for, it will not be there at the end. A person who builds his confidence on those networks alone is building on something the Book has already announced will be dismantled, and the announcement is the reason the verse says guard rather than prepare. The other side of the warning is the invitation hidden inside it. The Book says that no intercession will be accepted on that Day, and the clause presumes that intercession exists and that it is granted by permission, as other verses make clear. What is being denied is the presumption that a person can arrange it in advance by buying favour, hiring advocates, or resting on someone else's standing. The Book keeps the door of mercy open everywhere and closes the door of manipulation here, and the reader who wants the first must give up his reliance on the second.

**USING THE TIME THAT IS STILL NEGOTIABLE**

The practical force of the verse comes from the word guard, which is an instruction about the present. The Day being described is the one on which the accounts are settled, and the reader is currently living in the window in which the accounts can still be changed. The Book uses the same logic in its appeals for charity, where the appeal is attached to the same deadline: (2:254 — **“O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day”**), with the same list of unavailable helps following. Time is the only commodity in this verse that the reader still controls, and the Book treats its use as the whole content of a religious life. One matter left for later, whether a debt, an apology, or a habit, can be settled while the four doors are still open. The Book does not ask for a dramatic gesture here; it asks a person not to be among those who arrive at the Day relying on what that Day does not offer. A reader who acts on that in one matter has taken the warning seriously, and the warning is written in the language of a settlement rather than a spectacle precisely so that it can be acted on today. A final hearing is like a court in which borrowed influence, late payment and another person's record are all ruled out before proceedings begin. The advance notice directs effort toward the only account that will still belong to the person standing there.

---

## Verse 2:49

> ˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord

**THE YEARS UNDER A TYRANT, REMEMBERED BY THE ONE WHO ENDED THEM**

The chapter now walks the children of Israel through their own history, and it begins at the worst point: ***“˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh”***, ***“who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons”***, ***“and keeping your women.”***, and ***“That was a severe test from your Lord”***. The command to remember is placed on the rescue rather than on the suffering, which is the shape of the whole passage. The Book could have opened with the slavery, and instead it opens with the one who broke it. Even the final clause, which names the ordeal as a test, treats the test as something administered by the same Lord who is doing the delivering. The details of the oppression are reported without softening, because the Book wants the reader to know what the deliverance cost and what the alternative was. A regime that kills the sons of a people and keeps its daughters alive is managing a population rather than fighting a war, and the verse names the practice in a single clause. The same events are recounted in other sūrahs with more detail, and the pattern there is identical: the cruelty is stated, and the rescue is credited to God in the same breath. The reader is not being invited to admire a victim or to hate a nation; he is being taught to attribute his own escapes correctly. Al-Suddī described the torment as degrading labour joined to the killing of sons, while reports from Ibn ʿAbbās connect Pharaoh's policy to his fear of a child who would end his rule. The policy was therefore calculated oppression, not stray violence. Another passage names its public form: (28:4 — **“slaughtering their sons and keeping their women. He was truly one of the corruptors”**).

**THE SEVERITY THAT CUT BOTH WAYS**

The phrase about a severe test is easy to misread as a comment on the suffering of the enslaved, as though the Egyptians were an instrument of divine discipline. What the sentence actually names is the whole situation, and its severity cuts both ways. For the people being oppressed, the test was whether they would keep their faith in a God whose help was invisible for generations. For their oppressors, the test was whether they would recognise the authority that had raised them and used them. The Book reports both outcomes, and the second one is the reason the next verse is about a sea. The word for the test in this line is the same word the sūrah used when it spoke about the challenge of the Book and about the parable of the mosquito. In every case the test is a situation in which a person's direction is revealed, not a random misfortune. That consistency matters to a reader who is carrying his own trial: the Book treats hardship as a place where something is being decided, and it treats the outcome of the deciding as the part that lasts. The severe test in Egypt is named after the rescue rather than before it, which tells the reader where the sentence about hardship is going.

**READING A DELIVERANCE THAT HAPPENED LONG AGO**

For a reader who is not a member of that community, the verse asks him to look at his own escapes and to get the attribution right. Every life contains a few moments where the wrong thing was expected and the right thing happened: the illness that turned, the door that opened, the bullet that missed. The Book's habit is to name those moments as the favours of God, and the command to remember is aimed at exactly that. The point is not to replay the past but to keep a person from crediting his own cleverness for the ground he is standing on. A reader can put the verse to work by writing down one rescue from his own history and naming who arranged it. That is the same act the children of Israel were asked to perform with the exodus, and it is available to anyone with a memory. The Book wants the entry recorded correctly rather than a mood replayed, because a person who has forgotten who brought him out of Egypt will not recognise the hand that is carrying him now. The way a scar records both an injury and the healing that followed it, this inherited memory holds torment beside deliverance. Remembering only the wound breeds bitterness, while forgetting the wound makes the rescue appear ordinary. In modern life, oppressed peoples still face the choice between preserving a truthful rescue and turning an inherited wound into permanent identity.

---

## Verse 2:50

> And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes

**A ROAD THROUGH THE WATER**

The next item in the history is the escape itself: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you”***, and ***“and drowned Pharaoh's people before your very eyes”***. The sentence is short, and it holds three events that no human being could have arranged for himself: water standing where water does not stand, a people walking through it, and an army disappearing behind them. The Book reports the event elsewhere with the command that produced it, so the reader can see how the impossible was done: (26:63 — **“So We inspired Moses: “Strike the sea with your staff,” and the sea was split,”**). The rescue belongs to the one who issued the order, and the staff is credited with nothing beyond obedience. Al-Suddī carried the account of Moses striking the sea and the water opening into a road for the departing people. Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās likewise preserve the command to travel by night, which means the rescue joined revealed direction, human obedience and an opening no human power could make.

The closing phrase about the eyes is the detail that makes the verse a favour rather than a legend. The people did not hear about the drowning afterwards; they watched it happen from the far shore, which means the memory they were asked to keep was an eyewitness memory. That is why the command to remember carries such weight across the passage. The Book is not asking a later generation to believe a rumour; it is asking them to inherit a testimony from people who saw the water close. The same events are told in the sūrah of the Poets with the three stages separated into three sentences: first the sea was split, then (26:65 — **“and delivered Moses and those with him all together”**), and then (26:66 — **“Then We drowned the others”**). The reader is being shown a rescue in three movements, each of them credited to the same hand.

**A MEMORY A LATER GENERATION INHERITS**

The adult readers of this sūrah were not the ones who walked through the sea, and the Book still addresses them as the rescued. That is a pattern worth noticing, because it explains how a community carries an experience it did not have. The memory is passed on as a claim about who they are and who brought them there, and the passage expects each generation to adopt the deliverance as its own. A reader from any community can see the same mechanism at work in his own history, where the events that formed his people were mostly watched by people who are now gone. The purpose is not nostalgia, and gratitude is not treated as an emotion about the past. The exodus is placed here as the ground for the demands that follow in the chapter: the covenant, the law, and the warnings about forgetting them all rest on the fact that these people were slaves and were freed by someone who had no obligation to do it. A demand that looks arbitrary in isolation becomes proportionate once the history is remembered, which is why the Book keeps placing the history in front of the demand.

**WHAT TO BUILD IN THE SPACE A RESCUE LEAVES**

The practical side of the verse is that a person who has been brought out of something is expected to act like it. The Book does not require anyone to spend his life describing the experience, but it does require that the experience change what he obeys. A community that has been freed from a tyrant and then runs after other tyrants has learned nothing from its own history, and the sūrah will make exactly that accusation before the passage is finished. The test of gratitude in the Book is always the same: it is shown by what a person does with the freedom he was given. For a reader today the exercise is to name the thing he was delivered from and to ask what he has built in the space it left. The Book's expectation is modest and concrete, and the sūrah has already named the materials elsewhere in the chapter: prayer, charity, and the company of people who bow. A person who has been rescued and uses his freedom for those things has answered the command to remember, and the water he did not part has done its work in his life. Think of a causeway appearing where an army sees only water and a trapped people see no route. The opening becomes a road only for those who move at the command, and it closes on the power that trusted its own numbers.

---

## Verse 2:187

> It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺

## Verse 2:196

> Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination. ## Verse 2:217

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

## Verse 2:233

> ˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. If you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

## Verse 2:259

> Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, “How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?” So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life. Allah asked, “How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?” He replied, “Perhaps a day or part of a day.” Allah said, “No! You have remained here for a hundred years! Just look at your food and drink—they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!” When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything.”

## Verse 2:282

> O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing. Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties. The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write. They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt. If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice. Call upon two of your men to witness. If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness—so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her. The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned. You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺ for a fixed period—whether the sum is small or great. This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts. However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it, but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized. Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺. Be mindful of Allah, for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

## Verse 2:286

> Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford. All good will be for its own benefit, and all evil will be to its own loss. ˹The believers pray,˺ “Our Lord! Do not punish us if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord! Do not place a burden on us like the one you placed on those before us. Our Lord! Do not burden us with what we cannot bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our ˹only˺ Guardian. So grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”
